Dario only looked at it coldly, as if at a corpse. Fidela drew her sword on the spot to kill it. Had I not stopped her, this Seaborn would long be dead.
In the end, they all came to the same conclusion as you—it is the enemy.
How long has it been imprisoned here?
Here, sixty-three years. But if you trace back to when it came to Iberia, nearly a century.
Were there Seaborn causing havoc as far back as the Golden Age?
Havoc? No. It was once the Stultifera Navis's most precious trophy, a symbol of Iberia's great conquests. The old king chose the prince's name day especially to unveil it.
He even ordered his casters to inscribe alchemical formulae upon it and placed it at the heart of the shipyard, making it a vital force that drove this vast and intricate capital.
Wait... This Seaborn was once in the shipyard, used to power Rea-Iberia? Then...
One reason I assigned Fidela to the shipyard was so she could rest. The other was to place this Seaborn back in the shipyard—it is a part of salvaging the Central District.
I don't understand...
If you put High Inquisitor Fidela in charge of the shipyard, you must have meant for her to learn of this history.
She's seen this Seaborn before, too. You needn't worry that she couldn't handle receiving it. So why did you say it was for the best that Her Excellency didn't come?
Because the story of this Seaborn did not end with the Profound Silence.
Look down, Irene.
During the Profound Silence, a colleague of mine and I took this Seaborn away from the Port City. Not to cling to any memory, but to understand what it was we were about to face.
How ironic. We once treasured it, and later hated it to the bone—yet in the end, we still had to rely on it to light our way.
You never use empty rhetoric with us. "Light our way"... You mean our lanterns? But how is that possible?
What lights the lantern in your hand is still your unwavering conviction. You proved that aboard the Stultifera Navis months ago.
But conviction itself is no more than a set of abstract principles. What truly makes it undying is always human love and hatred.
...Just as my teacher loved this land so deeply.
And hated the Seaborn.
The casting unit embedded in that lantern cannot discern your creed, but it can read your most burning love and hatred.
After the Profound Silence, Iberians were afraid even to look straight at the sea, let alone exterminate the Seaborn.
The Inquisition selected the soldiers with the strongest will, and it owed them weapons fit for their hands. We needed a means to fight the sea, even if that means came from the sea itself.
So "an Inquisitor must face the Seaborn" isn't empty rhetoric either—
Because we must understand it, and then choose to hate it. Only then can the Arts be sustained, and the lanterns lit.
Yes.
If from now on it serves as Rea-Iberia's core, then...
The Arts that sustain the lanterns will not be affected immediately, but before long they will lose their original effect entirely.
From the moment it returns to the shipyard, the Inquisitors closely bound to their lanterns will feel their will waver ever so slightly, like a candle flame in the sea wind.
This will be the second trial they must undergo since resolving to become Inquisitors.
You may question me, or even challenge me here and now.
The moment I agreed to carry out the Salvage Plan, I had already considered every consequence—both those I must bear, and those Iberia must bear.
Su Santidad, I was only thinking that I now understand what you asked me in your office just now.
If Supervisor Clementia's will can become part of Ægir's will, then for Iberia, from now on, it need not be the Inquisition alone that lights the way.
And I've remembered something else.
Before I met my teacher Dario, I was just an ordinary child with a little training. I'd never even served in the Penal Battalion.
My teacher always said I was too devout, too loyal, too convinced that the Inquisition's scripture and laws were everything to me... In his eyes, that was my greatest weakness.
He hoped my sense of justice would be rooted in the sights my eyes had seen, the words my ears had heard, and the land my feet had walked—not in scripture and law.
I wish the same for all Iberians.
These people must silently recite scripture even just to choke down dried fin as hard as stone with a little less misery.
Yet these are also the people who, without even realizing it, will join a child by the roadside in singing a tuneless shanty.
Iberians should have the right to walk alone at night. The light should not belong to the Inquisition alone.
Now, Ægir has brought Iberia a chance to breathe on the front lines. A century of experience warns me that Iberia's time has always been precious.
Take this Seaborn away. And then, as on every day in Iberia, be prepared.
The Saint struck a match. Its light was bright and dazzling, in no way inferior to the Inquisition's pink lanterns.
The firelight illuminated the Seaborn's tangled, horrifying limbs. Soon it would leave the Inquisition's cage and return to the shipyard, to the place where it had originally been held.

Irene couldn't be certain whether lanterns no longer sustained by Arts could still hold back the Seaborn. Even less certain was whether, when the lanterns went out, the Inquisition's faith would be shaken.
But at least Irene could be certain that hers would not.
She had seen Dario fall in battle beneath the lighthouse. She had seen Jordi, introverted but resilient. She knew Iberians could do more—the night had simply shrouded them for too long.
She trusted Su Santidad's judgment. More importantly, having seen it with her own eyes and lived it herself, she trusted her own judgment, too.
For a while, I worried you wouldn't wake up, Nacho.
The joint between your arm and your prosthetic went without medical care and got infected long ago. You still have a fever. Rest for now.
Is this the church? You're Aquila's Mentor...?
Call me Aulus.
Mr. Aulus, Aquila's been arrested by the Inquisition. I don't know what happened, but a few days ago she told me that if anything happened to her, I should come find you.
So she had already made up her mind back then.
What are you talking about? Made up her mind about what? Can you help Aquila? She's so stubborn—if she angers the Inquisitors during the interrogation, it'll only get worse...
Nacho...
One moment.
Arrested... dungeon... Aquila...
Confirmed...? What do we do now...
I understand...
Aquila...
Nacho.
Aquila... What happened to Aquila?
Please don't make that face. That's the face the doctor made when he told me I'd lose my arm. It's the face Grandma made when she found out how sick she was...
I know why she kept so much from me, but could you please—
Nacho.
Aquila is dead.
What...
You're more patient than I imagined. In your plan, you're the one leading the Islanders.
Heh. Does analyzing all that make you feel safer?
Analyzing all that assures me that you very much want to get out of here and lead them to do what you believe is right.
"Right"... Then it sounds like we're no different from the Inquisition.
For the sake of what you call Iberia, you lump the Church of the Deep and the Islanders together, because that's the easiest way for you to do what's most right.
You can't deny that many Islanders have ties to the Church of the Deep.
I do know quite a few Islanders who joined the Church of the Deep. But do you know why they did it?
I had an Islander friend who fell in with the Church of the Deep. Before his execution, he confessed to me. He knew he'd done wrong, and he wasn't going to make excuses for it.
But he said that at least when he was with the cultists, he didn't have to lie awake worrying someone would smash his window. At least someone called him kin.
The Inquisition doesn't deliberately harm Islanders.
But you don't punish the people who do, either.
You and I both know what Iberia's "peace" rests on, and what "spices up" the dull, barren lives of Iberians.
I know a lot of kids who've had firebombs thrown at them. One of them lost his whole right arm.

I've known him since we were little. He's so kind he can't even bring himself to kill a fin. He can recite any passage of scripture. He's always trying to prove to everyone that Islanders are ordinary, decent Iberians too.
But even with a perfectly clear conscience, he still lives on edge. That's Iberia. The moment anyone mentions a crime, even Islanders themselves believe an Islander did it.
That is exactly why the Inquisition has preserved every dossier and record it can since its founding.
We record every word truthfully because we know how dangerous our work is, and in every interrogation, our virtue is put to the test.
Virtue... Fine. Even if I believe every recorded statement is true, how can you guarantee that every investigation involving Islanders uncovered the truth?
The truth?
You can't, and neither can I. We'll never know whether an Islander reported by a neighbor for deliberate harm and locked in a dungeon had once been bullied by that very same neighbor.
And we'll never know what truly started the hatred, or which way the scales of justice would really tip. In an endless cycle of hatred, we'll never be able to forgive each other.
The Inquisition has choices. You can choose to salvage the Port City and build a city that looks a bit more lenient toward Islanders. But I have a choice too. I choose to...
Keep hating.

Aquila looked at her hands. The edges of the crudely made handcuffs were sharp, and without her noticing, they had already cut her wrists. They seemed to mock the prisoner, as if they couldn't care less whether she lived or died.

Aquila knew her task was already done. All she had to do was keep it from the Inquisition. The best thing she could do now was wake up more Islanders—more people unwilling to speak of the wrongs done to them.
Sorry, she told her friends in her heart. She knew hatred wasn't a good choice, but it was the only choice that could unite them to do something.
Iberians should remember what Islanders once did, and what they've suffered. Even if it isn't me, other Islanders will stand up and take back what's rightfully theirs.
Most of your analysis was right, but one part was off. I don't actually want to leave this place, Your Excellency the High Inquisitor.
What?
Meeting my end here may be worth more to my kin who are still wavering.
Wait—!
She... killed herself?!
You look very sad. And angry, too?
...Aquila is dead, Mr. Aulus!
Of course... Of course you have reason to grieve. But why are you angry?
She always teased me for working too hard for the Iberians. But when we first came here, she worked far harder than I did.
I thought she was the one who still had hope for the future. I don't understand what made her throw all of that away.
I believe it's because she couldn't ignore what her kin were going through, Nacho.
So it's all because of this Mutual Aid Society, isn't it?
I've traveled all over Iberia. I know how painful it is to live in a place full of strife and prejudice. I wanted to do something for my kin.

I've seen villages vanish into the waves when the dikes broke, and graveyards piled with the starved. I've saved Ægir who were hunted down like prey, and I've persuaded wandering Islanders to go home.
And then I reached a conclusion.
What plagues Iberia today is not some sudden barrenness, nor the sea monsters of rumor, and certainly not the Islanders who are seen as an ill omen.
Tragedy happens simply because Iberia is a nation built upon strife, because it has never truly longed for peace.
I don't understand why you're telling me this, Mr. Aulus. Do you think Aquila did those things because she didn't want peace?
No. I only mean that people always use their position to bind themselves and discipline themselves. We are Islanders, they are Iberians, and those in the sea are the true Ægir.
Only once a person finds their position will they think for it, strive for it, make choices for it.
...So that's why Aquila always told me that the people in the Mutual Aid Society were our "real kin"?

Maybe that's also why I always felt I couldn't fit in with the atmosphere at the Mutual Aid Society. No matter how much everyone stressed who our "real kin" were, who the traitors and villains were...
It never made me feel any safer, and it never made things any better.
But what people describe having suffered is real. Perhaps Aquila once wanted to rebuild her life through the salvage work, but just hearing what her kin had been through...
Was enough to make her want to do something for them. So she made her choice. She died in prison, to keep a secret.
A secret...
Mr. Aulus, let me join the Mutual Aid Society.
I want to know what Aquila really died for.
(Delicate chewing)
(Elegant sipping)
...Do you have to observe noble etiquette even while eating, Tefi?
Shh. Some of the shipwrights have only just started believing in my noble title. I can't let all that effort go to waste.
This job wasn't easy to come by, Tefi.
I'll work hard. Just now even the foreman said I have a talent for learning ship blueprints. I really must be a descendant of the Iberian Royal Navy.
Recruiting supporters isn't going as smoothly, though... That Salvador just won't budge!
I've decided to change my story. I'll make him believe I'm the orphan of a legendary Saint who was descended from nobility, joined the Inquisition, and died a glorious martyr. What do you think?
Sigh.
All right, I know you don't like hearing this stuff. Tell me about yourself, Valerio.
Me?
Yeah. When we first teamed up, you were the one who said you wanted to come to the Port City. Lately I can never find you at the shipyard. Have you been looking for family?
After all these years, how could I find any family? They cut ties with me after I was injured.
That's awful. Even if burns are hard to treat around here, they can't just abandon you like that. And I remember you got hurt saving a friend, right? He doesn't care about you either?
It's all in the past.
It can't just be in the past! You might have forgotten, but I remember what you looked like the first time I saw you.
Today a ship sets sail♪
A fowlbeast paces on the rail—♪
Boss, the check.
*Cough, cough*... Sound the horn...
Stop singing, kid. Everyone's long gone.
Two copper coins. That's barely one meal.
There's half a glass of drink they left over there. Have it if you want. You've sung your voice hoarse.
Really? Thank you! The de Toledo family will remember your kindness!
Huh? There's still someone over there?
You won't get the price of a room out of him. That fellow's covered in burns, half-dead. Came in without a word, didn't buy anything, just leaned in the corner.
I hear he's been walking toward the coast the whole time, like a pilgrim. Can't think what holy place there is by the sea—there's nothing out there but sin. Best keep away from him.
If people keep any farther away from him, he won't even be able to beg a meal...
Oh, forget it. Skipping one meal won't kill me. Boss, two copper coins—get him something to eat.
The boss didn't give much. A piece of bread and a slice of ham thinner than paper. You spent the whole afternoon eating it, listening to me talk for half an hour every two bites.
There are lots of Iberians, and Iberians are all pretty much the same. But the only two who'd spend a whole afternoon on one meal just to con and be conned—that's us.
Yes.
So many Penal Battalion soldiers—what's going on?
High Inquisitor Fidela.
Mm.
You... look exhausted. There's even blood on the hem of your clothes... Have your injuries gotten worse again?
They just haven't gotten better.
Should we have a doctor reassess your condition? Perhaps you need medicine rather than rest.
Don't worry, it'll get better eventually. Besides, you've brought the thing that will cure my weariness, haven't you?
Inside this iron box is what Su Santidad wants the shipyard to take charge of—
The "key" that lifts the access lock on all the Port City's systems and keeps all of its city functions running?
Yes. Actually... actually, Su Santidad also said—
Good, good... Once the Central District rises above the sea again and Rea-Iberia reappears on Iberia's map, all the pain of the past will vanish like smoke.
Perhaps we should relearn the songs that were once banned, or even dance... Hm? What were you about to say?
No, it's nothing.
Tell Su Santidad to rest easy. I'll protect the shipyard and the hope in this iron box.
I swear it on my faith in the Inquisition and in Iberia.
Aquila's gone...
If it weren't for her, I might still be hiding at home every day, only daring to go out at night...
She's the one who recommended me to the Salvage Center. She always said it wasn't much of a job, but I know it's better than how things used to be.
She died for us.
She took on the riskiest part of the whole plan, and then she died in prison so the Inquisition wouldn't trace it back to us.
Now we have to finish the job.
Gaius...
If this kid thinks of himself as one of the Islanders, he won't talk.
Nacho, you grew up with Aquila. You don't want her to have died for nothing either, do you?
Gaius! That's going too far.
Am I not telling the truth?
Aquila's death shouldn't buy us this wishy-washy hand-wringing. Backing down won't make Iberia take us seriously. Bloodshed will.
Bloodshed... Our plan never included attacking Iberians directly!
But they started attacking us long ago. Don't you know how Nacho lost his arm? Among all the people burned or beaten to death in the streets, were there none of your own family or friends?
Our ancestors designed and built the Port City with their own hands, yet even now that it's about to see daylight again, not one Iberian remembers that.
On one hand they treat us as sinners who bring disaster, and on the other they want to claim the legacy our ancestors left behind... I'd rather that Central District stayed at the bottom of the sea.
That's right!
Tomorrow, we split up. Our target is the lighthouse array that powers the cranes.
Everyone get your diving suits ready. We go underwater—it's the fastest and most hidden route. I'll take Aquila's place.
Someone has already died for this. We cannot fail.
Understood.
You look even more confused.
Aquila meant to attack the lighthouse array and sabotage the Salvage Plan...
I guess I wasn't completely unaware. I just lied to myself that she worked so hard at the Salvage Center because she still had hope for the future.
I'm the one who never wanted to believe she'd been preparing for sabotage from the very start.
That's right.
When Grandma Rufina did those things back then, I didn't take part. When Aquila was making these preparations, I didn't take part either.
I thought that way, fewer people would get hurt.
But actually, even if I do nothing, everything still happens the same way, doesn't it?
Aquila, Grandma Rufina—they'll never stop struggling.
So they'll never stop getting hurt, either. Grandma died of illness, Aquila killed herself... I don't even know who I was trying to keep from getting hurt by standing aside and doing nothing.
Myself?
But I don't want to be the only one who comes out unscathed.
Aulus gently took hold of Nacho's right arm. The burn scars crawled hideously over his pale shoulder, glaringly obvious.
You haven't come out unscathed. The harm you've suffered torments you every day in the plainest way possible. But you can still decide who you'll bear this pain for.
You can join those Islanders and become one of the resistance. Or you can abandon them and become the Inquisition's helper.
Whatever you choose, Nacho, I promise you, I can heal your arm.
Heal my arm...
Nacho?
Supervisor Clementia.
You didn't come to the Salvage Center yesterday. I was worried about you.
I was trying to find some way to help Aquila. But there's no need anymore.
I'm so sorry. The Inquisition will issue a detailed account of the incident, if you want to know exactly what happened... Of course, if you'd rather not, I understand.
I'll go read it.
Tacita told me you were badly hurt when you came looking for me. So now—

Don't touch it!
No... I mean, it's fine now.
Fine?
A friend who knows some medicine took care of it for me.
If there's nothing else, I'll get to work, Supervisor Clementia.
Wait.
She took a tiny part from her pocket and placed it in the palm of Nacho's unharmed left hand.
Nacho recognized it at a glance. It was the bolt he had lost in the sea a few days before.
This...
The bolt you lost... Aquila found it.
Aquila...
When she was arrested, she asked someone to pass this bolt on to you. Whatever her reasons for those illegal activities, she still understood you, and cared about you.
Understood me... Yeah.
Supervisor Clementia, I told you how I lost my arm, didn't I?
Mm. You were hurt by a firebomb your neighbor threw out of malice.
But there's a first half to that story.

Grandma was one of the workers who built the Port City. Iberia should have honored her. But after the Profound Silence, merely not nailing her to a lamppost like other Islanders counted as Iberian mercy.
Everything she'd poured her life into for the first half of it was simply denied.
So she began organizing other Islanders who were just as unhappy. She wanted to prove the Islanders' innocence, their contributions, their worth.
It couldn't have gone well. What I saw was their methods becoming more and more extreme, more and more violent.

In the end, it seemed they couldn't find any other way. They started destroying the things Islanders had built with their own hands—the power cables Islanders strung, the wells Islanders dug, the crops Islanders grew.
But all they did was stir up even greater fear, and bring even more hatred down on themselves.
That firebomb...
Was originally meant to burn Grandma Rufina to death. Luckily, that day she happened to be out protesting and didn't come back until late at night. The only one asleep in bed was me.
Grandma worked for a month to make me a prosthetic. But our home had been searched by the Inquisition so many times that there weren't many usable parts left.
She held that one last bolt and just stared at me, dazed. I couldn't tell if she felt guilty, or sad.

After she finished the prosthetic, she fell ill and never got up again. Before she died, she called me to her bedside and stared at my hand in that same dazed way. I couldn't tell if she regretted it, or was sorry.
But one thing I'm sure of.
What she saw in this bolt was the same thing Aquila saw. Hatred.
The Mutual Aid Society... a church that opens its doors only to Ægir who are confused, suffering, and longing for peace.
Heh. Someone still uses lines like that these days. He must be very confident in his illusions.
Little Helper, scan the nearby blocks for any hidden buildings.
Command not recognized. Please first provide a definition of "hidden."
Tch, can't just use it like that, huh... Forget it.
We've circled two blocks already, and I've put together the Islanders' sighting reports.
Assuming the Mutual Aid Society is the starting point or end point of all their operations, then based on where Aquila dropped her air tank hose and the escape route from the last arrest...
There are five suspicious routes in total. Rule out the ones that pass checkpoints and the Inquisition's temporary posts, and that leaves three...
Searching— The three routes just walked intersect in only two places. One is the market. The other is an abandoned workshop.
Not bad. Better than Nando, anyway.
All right, get Clementia on the line for me. I've found a lead.
Get Clementia.
...Please contact Ms. Clementia, Supervisor of the Salvage Center, for me.
Command received.
Were you always this dense, or did Clementia spoil you?
Instructor Drusa.

*Ahem*! Supervisor Clementia, I've narrowed down the Mutual Aid Society's location to two places. One is an abandoned workshop on the seaside east of the district. The other is in the market next to the square.
But to be absolutely sure, I need more clues.
There's no time. I believe the Islanders in the Mutual Aid Society will make their move soon.
You want me to confirm their location tonight? It's doable.
But I suspect someone among them is good with Arts. Even if we raid tonight, chances are we'll have a hard time finding them. That said—
Their operation will become your clue to pin down the location.
Exactly.
Also, right now we still don't know whether their target is the Salvage Center or the power lighthouse array. The Inquisition is short on manpower. If it acts rashly, things could go wrong.
It's risky, but now that we've narrowed the Mutual Aid Society down to two places, playing along might pay off.
You think there's some other instigator behind the Mutual Aid Society?
Aquila was a resolute resister. If she had been leading the Mutual Aid Society, they wouldn't have waited this long to act.
I suspect there's someone else behind the Mutual Aid Society, someone better at scheming and soothing people's hearts—and that kind of person doesn't go out with the resistance.
Interesting. You want me to wait until the attackers have all left the nest and go pay him a visit at the Mutual Aid Society directly?
It's dangerous. Please be careful.
I know. But as for what happens next...
I'll keep Lord Iberia updated on our progress and have the Inquisition make sure the patrol units keep running as normal, watch the residential areas, and put the safety of the Iberian people first.
As for sabotage against the Salvage Plan—honestly, in my fifteen years as a Consul in Ægir, I ran into things like this nearly every month—
Ha... I am never going back to that "home" in the sea.
If you don't want to, you don't have to.
As for the attack, I'll help the Inquisition handle it.
I used to think the sea was the same every day.
Murky, stingy, endless. Wouldn't spare you so much as a single fin.
Turns out I just wasn't standing high enough. Every wave, every reef, every breath of sea wind smells different.
Please report today's sea conditions and lighthouse operating data, keeper.
Don't be so stiff, Elma. I know you envy my job. The view from up here looks nothing like the Iberia I knew for the first half of my life.
Shame we've still got a few days before the Port City's Central District gets raised. Right now there's nothing on the water but the ships sweeping the area.
And this freshly repaired power lighthouse smells like a new home. I wonder if the other thirty-six are the same—
Ramón! Report!
All right, all right...
Nothing's gone wrong in three months, and every lighthouse has a Penal Battalion squad on guard. You've got no reason to be so anxious. You woke me up when you left in the small hours...
8:49 AM, ocean monitoring report: coastal wind force 5, gusts to force 6. No storm surge detected.
It's a good day, ma'am.
...*bzzt*... ocean monitoring report... *bzzt*...
...coastal wind force... no storm surge detected...
(Opens a can)
(Chewing)
A can of fin, a shell fork, an ordinary Iberian breakfast.
Like any ordinary Iberian, he drank the juice from the can. The salt from the sea would give him the energy he needed.
...Lighthouse Seven... power supply system running stable...
...Thirty-One... dynamic load monitoring system activated...
...Fourteen... all communication signals normal...
(Washes the dishes)
(Washes out the can)
He put the fork away in a drawer, then set the can, filled with clean water, in the corner of the room.
A cloudbeast leapt in through the broken window, skirted the stones and shards of glass on the floor, and made its way to the water.
...Lighthouse... no change in personnel stationed at the power lighthouse...
...shift change in one hour... understood...
The seaweed hadn't dried long enough, so he couldn't bring it in yet. The window should have been mended three days ago—luckily, it hadn't rained lately.
He looked around the room, picked up only his fishing gaff, and left home.
The sea wind lifted the curtains. The mottled walls spoke for those who had once lived there.
(Struck-out Iberian scripture) "Rub salt into thy wounds. Pain is the proof of virtue, and leaves no place for the flesh of the alien to grow."
(Garbled Ægirian) They will not pardon. We will not forgive.
The sea's getting rough. It was fine when I reported an hour ago.
Scared?
I just don't want the hassle.

Sea conditions affect the power supply system. The Penal Battalion on guard is changing shifts, so we'll have to contact the checkpoint's comms officer ourselves and have them tell the Salvage Center to adjust the underwater work schedule.
Sigh. Once the Port City's Central District rises again, we can just sit back and count the sailboats on the water instead of doing all this tedious liaising.
Oh, come off it. I think you enjoy it—gives you a chance to chat with Elma on the clock.
Hm, that's not right.
Still trying to deny it? I heard your whole conversation just now from right here—
I mean the comms sound isn't right. Is our RF filter acting up? Why's the signal cutting in and out?
Oh, that's normal. It's been happening on and off for the last two months. It'll clear up in a minute.
Guess Ægir tech isn't all it's cracked up to be...

It's just not used to the local conditions. The Salvage Center's new Supervisor has already started optimizing all the technical components. The lighthouse power system hardware's getting upgraded in a few days too.
And worst case, we've got someone here to fix it. He's from the Salvage Center—what was that Islander's name again?
Don't remember.
Oh, perfect timing—here he comes.
Something's wrong... Ramón, call the checkpoint, now!
(Raises the fishing gaff)
How long has the signal been down?
Seven minutes.
The comms signals from all thirty-seven lighthouses were hijacked at once. The comms officers are still troubleshooting the equipment. We don't know yet which lighthouse was attacked to cause it.

There's one week left before the final salvage work. Attacking the lighthouse array that powers the cranes now—the attackers want to sabotage the Salvage Plan and drive a wedge between Iberia and Ægir...
What about the Penal Battalion stationed at the lighthouses?
Apart from the three squads closest to the checkpoint, we've lost contact with every squad.

Those three squads just got back. They all say they received an encrypted message from Inquisition headquarters ordering them to report to the checkpoint immediately and stand by. I suspect the other squads got false messages too.
The attackers wouldn't walk right into our hands. The lighthouses those three squads guard are too close to the checkpoint. They're most likely not the targets.
We must confirm the status of the other thirty-four power lighthouses immediately.
Sir, the power lighthouses are too spread out, and most of them are remote. We have no idea how many attackers there are, or which lighthouses they've actually breached...
Deploy everyone stationed at the checkpoint immediately. March along the waterways and check on the other thirty-four lighthouses.
Operations Unit One, head to the coast and watch for movement in the water. Don't let the Sea Terrors become a potential threat.
Unit Two, question people along the streets. Find reliable witnesses and get as clear a picture of the attackers' movements as you can.
Understood. What about the patrol units?
They'll stand by along their usual patrol routes. We've received instructions from Su Santidad: priority is eliminating potential threats in the streets and ensuring civilian safety.
But then we won't have enough people to reinforce the lighthouses. If the power supply system is destroyed, the plan to salvage the Port City's Central District will be completely...
Iberia shall surely reclaim its once-glorious heart.
Su Santidad.
But for now, even if the Salvage Plan is set back, we must keep the longstanding grievances between the Islanders and the Iberian people from being stirred up again.
What good to Iberia is a city that rises amid grievance and gloom?
Understood!
Move out. Order the comms team to keep troubleshooting the equipment and restore the signal as soon as possible. And...
Contact Supervisor Clementia. We need assistance.
What's going on? Why are so many Inquisition units marching past the shipyard?
And why did High Inquisitor Fidela say no one connected to the shipyard is to leave it for any reason? Has there been some kind of riot outside...
All right, all right, do you know why those Penal Battalion soldiers want us to stay here?

It's because we—the distinguished reserve force of the Royal Navy fleet—are far too intimidating to show our faces in a situation like this. Those Penal Battalion soldiers must have it completely under control, so they won't trouble us to go out.
"...I pray that ye wield the light of judgment... to cleanse our sinful bodies..."
Sigh, Salvador recites those lines all day long, and now everyone's picked them up... Wait, where is he?
I-I don't know. I haven't seen him since the commotion started outside.
Wait, Lady de Toledo, don't go looking for him. High Inquisitor Fidela said over and over...

I heard her. That High Inquisitor's voice is loud as an earthquake. But it also means the Penal Battalion at the shipyard won't move. Even if we report someone missing, they won't send anyone to look.
His family's all back in his village, waiting for the wages he earns fixing ships here. We can't let him just vanish without a word. He may not be a supporter of de Toledo yet, but...
Who's to say he won't become one of my followers later?
I'm going to find him.
So many Inquisition units... Why such a show of force today...
Hey, you.
Oh! O-officer, I already reported to an Inquisitor just now. The Islanders living here are all suspicious, they should all be searched, I—
Oh, so you reported me too?
An Ægir... in a Penal Battalion uniform...?
Sorry, I skip my shifts a lot. No wonder you've never seen me on the streets.
This is the block near the square. The people living around you are all Salvage Center technicians, right? Last night after curfew, did you hear anything going on outside?
N-no. They usually only go out early in the morning. And these past few nights, the fin-oil lamps in their homes have been burning bright. Nothing unusual.
You're sure of what you saw?
I'm a nervous sort... I check every day...
Nothing unusual. Good. Then this place is ruled out.
That leaves only—
This abandoned workshop on the seaside to the east.
A church that opens its doors only to Ægir who are confused, suffering, and longing for peace—give me some answers.
Who's hiding behind all this, and why are they stirring up my kin?
Where on earth did Salvador run off to? There's no one in his dorm, and he wasn't at any of the shops he usually goes to.
The streets are full of Penal Battalion units. Looks like they're dealing with Islanders causing trouble...
"...Saints above... I shall follow the guidance of the embodiment of Iberia's virtue..."
That's his voice!
The Saint will guide you?
Then if he told you that you had to die here today, would you agree to that too?
Who do you think you are... What right have you to speak for Iberia's holy ones?
"I pray that ye wield the light of judgment to cleanse our sinful bodies, and drive out the abominations born of sin."
Sinful bodies? Isn't the sin on us just something you forced onto us?!
Look out!
You're that Liberi who sang the shanty...
You remember me? Looks like the fame of this descendant of naval commanders has spread far and wide after all. Kin—
I'm not your kin!
Ah, now that's not right. Back in the Golden Age, Islanders and Iberians were partners. Islanders sailed with the Royal Navy fleet too!
Every Islander was talented, and they brought technology from the sea. What noble eager to win glory would refuse to take them under their banner?
De Toledo... A swindler thinks she can talk me around?
I'm not—
I remember you because that song was my lullaby when I was a child. But the family who sang it to me are gone now. Do you know where they went?
Uh... well...

If you're guilty of anything, it's not the pride and arrogance of the past. It's that you forgot, abandoned, even came to hate the people who were once your partners.
You need to pay the price—
Ugh...
Suspicious Islander found and apprehended. Wait, you're...?
We meet again, Mr. Nando. We're here because...

Su Santidad and Supervisor Clementia have ordered that the safety of the people in these blocks must be guaranteed. We just found explosives left by the attackers on a nearby street and disposed of them in time, but it's still not safe here.
I'll escort you back to the shipyard. As for disobeying orders and leaving the shipyard, High Inquisitor Fidela will deal with that.
You're actually pretty reliable when you're being serious... Thank you. Salvador, let's go.
Suspend all sea-sweeping work, and have the salvage workers who've already set out return at once!
Do a head count, confirm the location and movements of every shipwright, and make sure they're safe!
Sir...
My resignation as an Inquisitor has already been announced within the Inquisition. Just call me by my name, soldier.

Irene, we just got word from the checkpoint's comms officer. They're still confirming the situation at the lighthouses that were attacked. Every Penal Battalion soldier stationed in the Port City's Outer District has been deployed.
It's been half an hour since the lighthouses' comms signal was hijacked. Apart from a few workers suspected of taking part in the attack, everything at the shipyard is normal.
This place clearly isn't their target.
You want to lead the shipyard's garrison to reinforce the lighthouses?
Yes.
That's the fifth message in half an hour...

Even the patrol units who handle everyday public order are on emergency duty, and all we can do is guard a bunch of shipwrights who don't know anything, while turning down request after request for support from Inquisition headquarters.
I'll handle it.
Your Excellency Fidela...
High Inquisitor Fidela.
The shipyard's garrison will not be sent as reinforcements. That was my order.
Even if the entire power array is destroyed in the attack, the Penal Battalion under my command must hold their posts.
Seaborn?
Yes, the Penal Battalion must stay stationed at the shipyard. That's an order. What we're defending is Iberia's future.
I'll say it one last time: we will not be sending reinforcements.
Irene, you understand my duty.
Of course! Su Santidad put you in charge of guarding the shipyard—that's the best arrangement for the Salvage Plan. You need everyone at the shipyard to hold their posts. I understand.
But you're not one of the shipyard's people.
Ma'am?
And as an Inquisition Messenger, you have the authority to call up a squad in a state of emergency.

Soldiers who can't understand their orders find it hard to keep faith. I've been through everything they're going through now, so I know they don't want to watch their comrades die while they stand by helpless.
Take that Penal Battalion squad from just now and go reinforce the main force. If they want to die on the front line, that's their choice.
Yes, ma'am!
Hung up? Is it really that hard to get someone from the Inquisition to help?
These days High Inquisitors don't even hit the roof when they hear "Seaborn"? What earth-shattering task does the shipyard have that she doesn't care what a mess I'm in over here...

Seaborn specimens, alchemical instruments, and some collectibles from a century ago... Seems whoever's pulling the strings is getting on in years.
There seem to be a lot of passages in this workshop. Is that part of the illusion too?
Hm, what's this?
On the old floorboards, the black-haired Ægir found traces of nethersea brand that hadn't yet dried. They spread all the way to the end of the room.
Me and my big mouth...
(Slithers smoothly)
(Probes cautiously)
Which of you is the mastermind?
(Membranes flutter)
(Tendrils twist)
Just a joke—oh, but I guess you lot don't laugh.
Ugh, and there's a lot of them. I really hate people with so many tricks up their sleeves. Either he saw Clementia's and my plan coming, or he's as cautious as a musbeast.
As much as I'd love to just walk away, your being here at least proves one thing—whatever that mastermind's after has something to do with the Seaborn.
Looks like I'll have to bring Clementia a souvenir.
The Ægir flicked the coiled "sash" at her waist. It was supple as a Seaborn's tentacle, yet it rang with a crisp metallic sound. This weapon rarely left its sheath, but it was impeccably maintained.
The Seaborn could never understand that the one standing before them was an instructor who had honed herself in real combat—and honed countless Penal Battalion soldiers as well.
Hope she doesn't mind if the present comes in too many pieces.
Supervisor Clementia, Su Santidad has arrived at the checkpoint and is directing the operation.
Our preliminary assessment is that the attackers are Islanders with grievances against Iberia. They're attacking the power lighthouses in order to sabotage the Salvage Plan.

Comms still haven't been restored. The thirty-seven lighthouses that make up the power array are scattered across the coast, the hills, and elsewhere around the Port City. Our search has been badly hampered.
We need your help.
How long has it been since comms went down?
Twelve minutes.
If the Islanders' goal is to destroy the power lighthouses, we don't have much time left.
The power lighthouse array is vital to the Salvage Center. Damage to any one lighthouse will affect the cranes' output.
We need to know their numbers and their movements.
If we pull the power supply system's reports, could we find clues in the data?
If there were clues in the power supply system, it would already be throwing errors.
Damn it. All we can do now is wait for the squads stationed at the lighthouses to regroup at the checkpoint to get more information, but that'll take too long.

The patrol units found and disarmed several explosives scattered around the streets. The attackers seem intent on causing even more chaos. But beyond that, there are no other clues anywhere in the Outer District.
If they've been planning this for so long, they must have left some trace, even if that trace isn't on land, but in...
In the sea?
A sound—no, a tremor in the water—came from the deep sea several kilometers away, stirring the neuromasts of her lateral line and sending a shiver across her skin.
Even without sight or limbs, the sea's information kept flowing toward her, gathering where she was. She could feel everything.
...Clemen... tia...
...Can you hear me... my little manta ray...
Horatia...
I didn't know piloting a ship through neural cables could be addictive. Good thing I can handle your unique driving style, or I'd have collapsed during the last jump.
Still not sleepy?

If piloting a ship could put me to sleep, I wouldn't have whisked the Institute of Scientific Development Planning's finest Consul off in a little floating pod in the middle of the night—who, as it happens, also couldn't sleep.
So, where are we now?
At the edge of Ægir's signal coverage.
Fifteen meters farther north, and we'll be completely out of range, cut off from the home territories.
A nice way to unwind. Drifting between the clamor and the silence, keeping our nation at arm's length for a while, so as to see it more clearly.
If it weren't for the insatiable Seaborn, you'd still be able to pick up Ægir's signal even dozens of nautical miles farther on.
Setting aside the Seaborn eating away at our cities, I think it's just right as it is. Do you want all of Terra to hear Ægir's voice?
That's our duty, isn't it? Ægir's current state is proof enough that we're the nation closest to the future, the one with the best hope of escaping destruction.
I have no doubt that once the Waterway Program succeeds, you'll issue a statement to the nations on the land of Terra—and they'll certainly think Ægir arrogant.
Humility won't bring success. It'll only slow us down.
We had this same conversation last month, only that time it was in a meeting room at the Institute of Scientific Development Planning.
You served in the Exercitus, then went from city to city as a Consul. I have no doubt of your love for Ægir. But whenever we talk about these topics, you always look hesitant.
I haven't reached a conclusion yet, Horatia.
But I'm certain of this: just as you like to stare at a detailed map of Terra when you rest, pondering how Ægir should cooperate with those nations, how to solve the ultimate question—
I like to be alone in a small floating pod, connected to the neural cables, letting all the information recorded by the beacon launchers flood into my brain.
Even at such a distance, I can still hear the busy tones of calls waiting to connect, lullabies, and the low cries of Seaborn lurking in their caves.
I think, before I loved Ægir, perhaps what I loved was this ocean.
Clementia gazed out of the floating pod. The light of the twin moons soaked into the boundless sea, diluted to the faintest glow.
Layer upon layer of shimmering light enveloped the two in the pod, like the neural cables on Clementia's fingers, lighting up countless tiny points of light.
She was tracing her Ægir with her own mind, feeling the information the sea passed to her—of the past, and of the future.
Information in the sea...
If we pull not just the power supply system's data, but every ripple the sea itself has felt, we might find a breakthrough.
Ripples in the sea? How is that possible...
The system of Milliarium's beacon launchers shares the same lineage as the lighthouse system on the Iberian coast. That's the physical foundation the joint land-sea defense line was built on.
Time shows no mercy to anyone. No matter how careful the attackers were, the longer they prepared, the more traces they left behind.
If we can get all the data the beacon launchers monitored, we can reconstruct every signal disturbance along Iberia's coastline and find where the lighthouses were attacked.
But Supervisor Clementia, Milliarium is very far from the Salvage Center. The signal will probably be extremely weak. And even if we can pick it up, how could anyone sift through that much data?
Leave it to me, sir.
The gentle former Ægir Consul gave the soldier a reassuring pat on the shoulder, then took a vial of some unknown drug from the pocket at her side and drank it in one go.
Clementia's expression was perfectly ordinary, as though she'd merely straightened her skirt. Only then did the Penal Battalion soldier notice that she wore unusual metal sheaths on her fingers.
They weren't weapons, nor were they for protection. The neural cables attached to the finger sheaths glowed and pulsed to some rhythm, as if breathing, or thinking.
I'll listen to the voice of Iberia.
Little Helper, contact Gladiia for me. I need to access the information from Milliarium's beacon launchers.
Consul Clementia—oh, no, I suppose it's Supervisor Clementia now. Long time no see.
I know you'd much rather see Swordfish, but the Captain's dancing with a huge crowd of Seaborn in their nest right now. She's really quite busy.
Hm, why are there so many people around you? Just a moment, I've only just finished a mission and haven't had time to tidy my skirt and hair—
There we go.
Thank you for your hard work, Hunter.
How kind of you. What do you need me to do? From the little I know of Supervisor Clementia, you didn't go and invite trouble right through your own front door, did you?
I need to borrow your data transmission privileges in Milliarium. Send me all the information the beacon launchers have detected over the past week.
Wow, all of it? Every rising tide, every ocean current, every flick of a fin's tail gets compiled into data stored in the beacon launchers. That's no small amount.
Which terminal should I send it to?
Here.
Clementia lightly tapped her temple with a finger connected to the neural cables.
That's not a very funny joke... I don't need to remind you that your central nervous system could very well shut down from bioelectric signal overload, do I?
We haven't talked much, but I'm personally rather fond of you. Besides, I'd hate to be charged with murdering one of my kin—
Ah, but then again, from the Seaborn's point of view, we've been carrying that charge for years.
Don't worry. The Exercitus the Abyssal Hunters are attached to falls under Milliarium's jurisdiction. I'll contact the Acting Consul to clear you of any suspicion.
If you stay alive, there won't be any suspicion to clear.
Rest assured, I will.
One second. Perhaps two.
The moment the call ended, the Salvage Center's monitoring panels and a dozen-odd Little Helpers all froze for an instant, like passersby standing before a tsunami with nowhere to run.
Clementia felt her fingertips grow faintly hot. The points of light on the neural cables pulsed frantically, leaving her just enough time to take one last deep breath—
Before she was thrown into the boundless sea of a week ago.
She opened her eyes underwater and gazed at the pitch-black ocean formed by a colossal stream of data.
The sea had never been so clamorous.
The blades of Ægir's city engines turned without pause. Hunters passed through swarms of Seaborn. Escort ships adjusted their headings, leaving tiny eddies behind...
But she had no time to dwell on her city, her home.
Countless pieces of information washed over her body. Clementia knew her perception was sliding into chaos, and her eyes were burning.
As she had countless times while drifting on the sea far from Ægir, she listened to everything—even a tiny electrical signal, or a single disturbance in the water.
At the edge of the vast ocean lay the blurred boundary between Ægir and Iberia, the farthest reach of the beacon launchers—and the place closest to the answer.
Clementia believed the sea would carry its dwellers ever upward, upward.
Until they leapt from the water, until...
*Gasp*...
Supervisor Clementia! Are you all right? Where's the medical squad?!
Lighthouses... Eight... Seventeen... The signal on their power cables... flickered out once three days ago...
I heard bubbles flowing through the pipes... It was our equipment... It was those poor, hate-filled people...
The anomalous data has been filtered out... and compiled into a report along a timeline... You can compare it with the suspects' movements...
Thank you, Supervisor Clementia. But you're... covered in cold sweat, your breathing and heart rate are too fast, like you're short on oxygen...
Go.
...Understood.
How much progress is left?
Thirty percent.
The entire power lighthouse array uses the same optical assistance system. It's an indispensable part of the power supply system, and it's also the Inquisition's eyes.
Once they've lost their sight, the Inquisition will have a hard time pinpointing us.
And an hour ago, we hijacked the lighthouses' comms signal. The Penal Battalion units have to set up temporary channels between themselves, which buys us more time.
I see Inquisition lanterns on the coastline!
That's impossible!
We've been careful. We shouldn't have left any trace.
Lighthouse Seventeen? Calling Lighthouse Seventeen!
Damn it!

Our kin on lookout sent word—the Penal Battalion is marching fast. They seem to have pinned down our location already. I—
Urgh!
Save your tongue for defending yourself in the Inquisition's dungeon.
Seal off the lighthouse!
Supervisor Clementia has confirmed the locations of the lighthouses that were attacked, and the Penal Battalion has arrived on the scene. We need to wrap everything up.
Remember, don't release the details of this operation to the public for now.
Understood!
(Sounds an alarm)
This is... Supervisor Clementia's Little Helper?
(Rotates its towing module)
You dragged this injured person over here? Wait, she's...
...Get Clementia for me.
Instructor Drusa!
*Pant*... *pant*...
Good thing we left ourselves a way out. Let's go, quickly.
But the mission isn't finished yet!
Just go, you've been bleeding this whole time.
We can only hide here for a while. Those Inquisition capullos will find us sooner or later.
But if this keeps up, before the Inquisition even catches you, you'll already be...
Press down on the wound. I'll get you out of here.
Nacho? What are you doing here...
Don't talk, Gaius. You've lost a lot of blood. Let me bandage you first.
Not... not as much as that Inquisition capullo I stuck in the thigh with my fishing gaff... *Hiss*!
Sorry, I pressed a little too hard.
I'll take you out underwater.
You've chosen to stand with us?
No. I just don't want to see any more Islanders die in prison full of rage like Aquila did.
Resistance always comes with sacrifice.
At least right now I can save you, and keep you alive until a turning point might come.
Let's go.
Phew... Apart from the ones the Inquisition took away, everyone else is here.
Th-thank you...
You saved fourteen badly wounded kin, all by yourself? And you carried them out through the waterways... It's nothing short of a miracle...
A miracle...
I just couldn't stand by and watch our kin get left out there to bleed to death. A lot of people hid themselves really well so the Inquisition wouldn't arrest them.
Soledad, when I found you, that wound on your leg looked really bad. Has the bleeding stopped?
Mr. Aulus already took care of it for me. But what about you...

Aquila always used to go on about how your arm was hurt too badly for you to go into the water at all. And now you've not only gone in, you've gone back again and again and brought all these people out... Shouldn't you have him take a look at you too?
The exhausted young man drew his hand away from his companion's touch, as though he were afraid he might hurt her.
Don't worry, Soledad. I've already had Mr. Aulus treat my arm.
Whatever you choose, Nacho, I promise you, I can heal your arm.
Heal my arm...
Mr. Aulus, there's no turning back for everyone in the Mutual Aid Society now, is there?
You could try to talk them out of it, but it will be difficult.
I understand. I lost count of how many times I begged Grandma Rufina to stop doing dangerous things, but she'd still slip out at night.
What Grandma did, what Aquila did... to me, it still seems too extreme.
But after joining the Mutual Aid Society, I understood one thing—I'll always be one of the Islanders. I want to help them, but in the state I'm in now...
Mr. Aulus, can you really heal my hand?
Good child.
My method of treatment is somewhat unusual. If you've made up your mind, come with me. And if you find the process hard to bear, you're free to refuse.
Perhaps it was because Aquila's death reminded Nacho of Grandma Rufina. Perhaps it was because the fervor in the faces of his kin in the Mutual Aid Society both stirred him and frightened him.
Even though he sensed something dangerous about the gentle man before him, he resolutely placed his wounds in the man's care. In that moment, only one thought filled his mind—
He couldn't let his kin all die full of hatred and regret. He wanted two healthy arms to stop them, or to save them. If Aulus could make that happen, he was willing to pay the price.
A slick, slimy sound reached his ears. He stared hard into the darkness of the workshop. A shadow stood silently not far away. Slowly, strangely, it drew closer to him.
That's...
Shh—
You're bound to be afraid. This is the sin and the monster the Inquisition wrote of in its scriptures—the one and only reason you're not allowed near the sea.
But rest assured, this individual... it's the work I'm most pleased with. It's the embodiment of everything I've achieved in decades of research.
It doesn't rage, doesn't quarrel, doesn't weep, doesn't do violence. Nor will it try to turn you into one of its own.

I rewrote the logic by which its neural signals are transmitted, so that it's less susceptible to the will of "the Firstborn." It still retains the ability to assimilate other organisms, but it no longer has the motive to do so.
Of course, the will of "the Firstborn" is carved into its genes. It will still stubbornly try to grow new neural tissue to replace the parts I've tampered with...
But as long as I intervene diligently, the process won't move so quickly.
If you doubt my words, we can stop the surgery at any time. The Seaborn are savage, monstrous things you can't reason with—that's what every Iberian believes—
No, I understand.
Oh?
I've also spent nearly twenty years trying to prove to the Iberians that Islanders are harmless, that we're not aggressive... But I didn't try hard enough. There was too little I could do.
Please go on with the surgery, Mr. Aulus. I can't afford to pass out again on my way to get help.
Smooth tentacles crept up Nacho's fingertips. The prosthetic, which shouldn't have had much feeling at all, was trembling.
He had seen what was left of fin-fishers after Sea Terrors attacked them. He fought with everything he had not to pull his hand back, and then—
The pain truly vanished.
(Membranes flutter euphorically)
Remarkable, Nacho. You're even calmer than I imagined. With no one to guide you, you've grasped the essence of sharing.
Sharing... Mr. Aulus, you keep company with the Seaborn, but you don't seem like some raving heretic. What is it you really want?
What I want is a true "utopia."
Nacho, tie the bandage a bit tighter for me.
It can't go any tighter, Gaius. Tightening it more won't stop the bleeding any better. It'll only hurt you.
But it'll drown out the pain of the wound. Our operation can't end here...

What are you talking about? Half our kin in the Mutual Aid Society have been arrested by the Inquisition, there are more and more Penal Battalion soldiers patrolling the streets, and we've got plenty of wounded. Stop this!
Before the operation, every one of us swore an oath. We'd make Iberia remember us. We'd make the Inquisition and all those Iberians who humiliated us regret it.
Islanders aren't tools for the Inquisition to summon and dismiss whenever they like. We'll make every Iberian fear us, and then we'll earn their respect.
It's not time to stop yet... Ngh... *Iberian curse* Get up, Gaius, get up!
Gaius, calm yourself.
Mr. Aulus, please talk some sense into them!
My kin, your resentment and hatred keep your wounds from closing. That is the price you must bear, and it is also a warning.
Mentor, you know every one of us and what we've been through. You know exactly why we're fighting back.
The Iberians threw my child to his death down a dry well. They thought it would calm the sea's wrath and bring in a bigger catch... But all it got them was my wrath.
Apart from me and my wife Ángela, who's going to remember that atrocity? Who's going to remember our innocent child?
Even if I lose both legs, I'll still knock on my enemies' doors. Even if I lose my voice, I'll still tell the world what they did!
Is this your choice?
It is.
And is it yours as well?
It is.
Very well.
Mr. Aulus...?
What happened to the church...
The church was a well-meaning disguise, and a way to keep the Inquisition from finding the Mutual Aid Society.
Now, faith cannot solve your problem, my kin. And every choice has its price.
I can heal the pain in your body. I can even let you forget all the torment you've endured—so long as you're willing to share.
Share?
What is that?! It's a monster from the sea! Mentor... No, you're with the Church of the Deep!
Don't be so tense. It won't hurt you. Neither will I.
Gaius, get away from that thing! It'll eat you till there's nothing left! I've seen it once... I've seen it...
It can let me stand again, and do more, right?
Yes. But if you do this, I'm afraid it will be very hard for you to see your wife again.
As far as she's concerned, I died the moment our child did.
A Seaborn that had appeared without warning in the workshop, and an Ægir who had already made up his mind. Amid the terrified, worried, angry, grieving crowd, they gazed at one another.
The stern, cold-faced man pressed his lips tight and clenched his fists, struggling to keep his body from shaking as he approached the monster. But everyone in the room knew that he was afraid too.
The instant the Seaborn touched him, his rigid body went slack. His eyes went vacant, yet a smile crept onto his face, as if a sight only he could see had appeared before him.
He wept. He reached out his bloodied arms and embraced the monster in front of him—as if he were embracing the child he could never hold again.
No... This isn't right! You said the surgery was harmless! I'm still fine, so why is Gaius—
He's still your kin. And now he can stand up and do what he wants to do.
If the rest of you don't want your wounds and illnesses to stop you here, I can help.
I don't want to become like that... I just wanted a slightly better life in this land, not...
These monsters are the very reason the Iberians spit on us and treat us like the root of all disaster! I can't, I can't have anything to do with things like that...
Have you all forgotten why you joined the Mutual Aid Society in the first place?! We're going to make the Inquisition and the Iberians face what we've been through, no matter what it takes!
Everyone's choices are different. Only those who share the same ideals can walk together.
What Gaius sought was different from what you sought, so the result of the surgery was different too.
I thought you'd help us, but not like this...
I respect everyone's wishes, Nacho.
I'm leaving.
Of course. The doors here will always be open to any Ægir who is lost, suffering, and longing for peace.
You may go and do whatever you wish. Anything at all.
Matters surrounding the attack are still being dealt with, and the lighthouse array will need time to be repaired. But the people's panic has gradually subsided.
I should thank you, Supervisor Clementia. You found the location of the lighthouse that was attacked for us, and spared us a great many losses.
As head of the Salvage Center, it was only my duty.
Besides, you and I both know the true heart of the Salvage Plan isn't the lighthouses.
Thirty-seven guard units—that alone makes the importance of the power lighthouses self-evident. Naturally, any malcontent bent on sabotaging the Salvage Plan would make them a target.
No one would ever imagine that a shipyard for salvaging and repairing wrecks is the true heart of the plan. That is where the Port City's central control room lies.
Navigation, power, communications—nearly every function of the Port City as a mobile city is controlled from there.
The most important of them is a vast sea chart system that once sustained nearly all seafaring in the Golden Age.
It records every city and town, every port that ever existed on Iberian soil, and every island and every fishing ground discovered by generation after generation of sailors.
Yet today, in all the Inquisition's vast archives, you would not find a single accurate, complete map of Iberia.

The blueprints the Islanders brought ashore back then should already include most of the functions of the Ægir sea chart system. It ought to be able to receive signals from cities and facilities and mark their positions in real time.
In a few days, when the Port City's Central District is salvaged and brought ashore, its coordinates will light up on the sea chart systems of Iberia and Ægir at the same time.
Indeed. And before the Islanders plotted their attack, the shipyard had already taken delivery of the "key" that can lift the system's access lock and restart the sea charts—
A Seaborn that belongs to the past. It will remain at the shipyard, and through the alchemical formulae within its body, it will keep all of the Port City's functions running normally.
...At least until we're able to rebuild all of the Port City's systems and functions ourselves.
So, you recruited shipwrights and sailmakers far and wide to throw people off the scent, and stationing High Inquisitor Fidela at the shipyard was a second safeguard.
When the lighthouse was attacked and the entire Inquisition was mobilized, she held the shipyard with her own unit.
Following orders is a soldier's duty, but I also know that watching her comrades take action while being unable to support them must have been agonizing for her.
I know my student. She is far too loyal to the Inquisition. Until all is settled, she will not know what it is she's been entrusted with.
Once Rea-Iberia is officially back in service, I will reveal the truth of the light to the members of the Inquisition. One day, they will have to kindle their lights anew with their own will.
It will not be easy.
Now, Supervisor Clementia, though we must still investigate what lay behind the Islanders' attack and track down the true instigator...
The salvage operation has truly taken another step forward. We may all breathe a little easier for now.
I hope so.
Su Santidad, Supervisor Clementia.
According to word from the checkpoint, an Islander who claims to have taken part in the lighthouse attack has appeared by the sea.
He wants to... turn himself in to the Inquisition.
On the black shingle of the shore, the sea wind wailed.

The first time he crawled ashore here, the one waiting for him on the beach was his grandmother. Grandma always walked fast, and he could only stumble along behind her, answering her endless questions.
Later, it was Aquila. Aquila would wrap a towel around him, and the two of them would stagger back across the shingle without a word.
And now, he couldn't even count how many Penal Battalion soldiers stood here to greet him. Their halberds were leveled at him in perfect unison, and the cold light glinting off them stung his eyes.
Among them, of course, was a figure he knew well.
Nacho...
I'm sorry, Supervisor Clementia. I've fallen so far behind on work lately.
Officers of the Inquisition, I confess to taking part in the lighthouse attack.
As long as you agree to my demands, I'll tell you everything I know.
Supervisor Clementia, the Inquisition has approved your request. You may now interrogate the Islander, Nacho.
Thank you.
Wait!
I knew you'd follow me, Tacita.
Supervisor Clementia.
If you're worried, I can promise you that I'll strictly abide by the principles of intervention I laid out in my proposal for salvaging the Port City.
In fact, I'm handling Nacho's situation the Iberian way right now.
Supervisor Clementia, no matter what assurances you give, I'll still be concerned for Ægir's interests. You can't convince me.
But I've also thought over everything you said. If I have doubts, I can go and verify them, and resolve them, myself.
That's right.
I'd like to sit in on this interrogation, Supervisor Clementia.
I want to truly understand what kind of people these Islanders are—our kin on land, whom you care about so much that you're even willing to take risks for them.
I understand.
Officer, would it be all right if I brought one more person into the dungeon with me, as a recorder?
Sorry, could the interrogation start as soon as possible? Some of my fellow Islanders are badly hurt. They need proper medical care, and—
What?
No, it's nothing.
Requesting permission to speak with you took some time. I have to respect Iberia's procedures.
Go on in, Supervisor Clementia. I'll step out.
Supervisor Clementia, Ms. Tacita?
Tacita will be recording our entire conversation, and I'll be the one questioning you.
I thought they'd send an Iberian Inquisitor.
You could barely get a word out in front of the Penal Battalion. If it were an Inquisitor sitting here, would you be able to tell them what you really think?
You've been watching me this whole time?
I'm just good at recognizing people who need help.
You and your kin are in trouble, aren't you?
We've been in "trouble" since the day we were born Islanders.
It's just that this time, Aquila's arrest and her death have forced me to face that "trouble" again.
Some of the Islanders who took part in the lighthouse attack are my coworkers or friends, so I know very well what they did before they were labeled attackers.
They brought electricity to abandoned towns, dug wells in dried-up land, raised crops that could grow in saline soil...

They wanted to prove they had the worth to live on this land, that they had the right to. But in the end, the way they chose was to destroy what they and their ancestors had built with their own hands.
The original lighthouses were designed by Islanders, and the Port City's thirty-seven lighthouses today really were all built by Islanders too.
If only everyone were like you, and still remembered what they'd contributed even after they made a mistake. Maybe then, none of what happened today would have happened.
But the fact that I'm here at all proves things have already gotten very bad.
You're a little different from before.
In these few days since I joined the Mutual Aid Society, I've kept thinking about what Aquila did, and even what Grandma Rufina did back then.
I used to keep my distance from the Mutual Aid Society because I believed spreading hatred was wrong—that the vicious cycle that cost me an arm was wrong.
But in the end, the conclusion I reached was that I don't actually care that much whether what they did was right or wrong.
After losing Grandma Rufina, after losing a friend like Aquila, only one thing is on my mind—I don't want to lose a single fellow Islander more to old grudges.
Nacho...
Call it some kind of psychological escape, or a moral failing called selfishness—whatever it is, I can't go against what I feel.
More than the officers of the Inquisition, more than the Iberians who look at Islanders so coldly, I simply understand how my fellow Islanders feel. This broken arm reminds me of that every moment.
Only now do I realize it wasn't my kin's bitterness that drove me away from the Mutual Aid Society. I was afraid of becoming another Grandma Rufina—afraid of hurting the people who matter to me.
But now I have nothing left to lose. For the sake of my kin, I'll ask anyone I can reach for a way out—as long as they don't hurt my friends.
I understand. Tell me your demands, Nacho.
I know who organized the Mutual Aid Society—who Aquila's "Mentor" is. I've seen him with my own eyes, and I'm almost certain his goal isn't just to help the Islanders attack the lighthouses.
I want to trade what I know about him for the lives of all the Islanders.
Silence—
All shipyard workers, I'm sure you've heard of the attack a few days ago. But rest assured, the Inquisition has already arrested the attackers, and the Salvage Plan will not be affected.
You will have the chance to take on far more glorious work than merely clearing the sea or repairing old ships.
From today on, you will have only one shared goal—to safeguard the salvage of the Port City's Central District in a few days' time, and to make Rea-Iberia a harbor of the land once more.
Now, I will reassign everyone's duties.
Abilio, take your crew and reinspect the cranes along the underwater corridor. Bursa, Elbio, have your teams report to Dock Three.

On the day of the salvage, the sea chart of Iberia will appear in the Outer District's plaza for the first time in sixty-three years. All the residents will see the dimmed coordinates of Rea-Iberia light up once again.
A sea chart? We're finally going to see how many cities Iberia used to have, and where they all were?
Before I came to the shipyard, I never thought I'd get to see something like that... Salvador, I guess you could say we're bringing the Port City back to Iberia with our own hands.
Shut your mouth. Don't forget why we're here.
We receive the Saint's grace and obey his will. All that we do is to prove our purity to the very embodiment of Iberia's virtue.
We ought to give, even to spend ourselves. We need not ask the reasons behind the decisions of the holy, nor reward ourselves with fine words.
Tefi, why are you only coming back now? Her Excellency the High Inquisitor was just about to call you to account—
What's wrong?
When the shipyard was locked down, I noticed Salvador was gone, so I went out to look for him. An Islander had him cornered in an alley, and he was clutching a rosary.

That's when I remembered—this morning at the shipyard, he suddenly started praying toward the church. We tried to talk him out of it, but he wouldn't listen. He must have left the shipyard to go home and get that thing.
The Islander cornering him had a fishing gaff and a murderous look on his face, but Salvador only had eyes for his rosary. He didn't care one bit about the danger right in front of him.
I know that if I hadn't shown up, he would have died for sure... died for his faith.

But I also know that the only reason he believed in all that in the first place is because he happened to sneeze just as the priest who was giving him charity was reaching into his robes to get him some food.

When he opened his eyes, there was a piece of unleavened bread in the priest's hand. He thought the priest could conjure food out of thin air, and that's how he muddled his way into becoming a believer.
And now he's willing to die for that faith?
I can't let him keep believing blindly like this. Su Santidad is so far away from him—how is he supposed to hear his prayers?
If he believed in Lady de Toledo instead, then even if I'm just a con artist, at least I could keep an eye on him and stop him from doing anything stupid. I could save him!
But what am I supposed to do...
Tefi, the statue, the uniform, the sword, the staff—and your stories—they worked because people want to believe in things that are new and interesting.
Right. Who in Iberia would want to believe some nobody with no power, no money, and no talent?
Then go and become "somebody."
What?
Even if it's just one thing that everyone's watching, it'd prove you're not all talk. Maybe then he'd believe you.
Salvador, what if I prove to you that I can be the one who lights up the sea chart?
Would you be willing to throw away everything you used to believe in, join my naval fleet, and believe in me?
What fairy tale are you spouting now...
Quiet! I will personally oversee every operation of the sea chart system, and at the salvage celebration I will light up—
Wait! High Inquisitor Fidela, please let me start up the sea chart and light up Rea-Iberia's coordinates!
Wha...
Disobeying orders, leaving without permission, disturbing public order, obstructing the official business of the Inquisition—do I need to list more charges?
If not for my mercy, you'd be in a cell right now.
But for the salvage to go smoothly, you're short on hands, aren't you?
What the shipyard is short on is shipwrights for the salvage, not some spectator on a whim. Starting up the sea chart isn't a matter of pushing a button.
I know.
You know?
In Stonesurge, I have a supporter whose ancestors once served in Rea-Iberia.
He said that a golden sea chart would fill the whole sky above the Outer District's plaza, so that everyone passing by could see the full expanse of Iberia's territory and be proud of it.
After the Profound Silence, Iberia's lands were broken into pieces. No one remembers anymore how many cities were once built on this land, or how many lie asleep beneath the water.
But I do.
I've traveled every corner of Iberia. I've chatted away with thieves, vagrants, Calificadors, even the descendants of nobles. I've committed every inch of land Iberia ever had to memory.
Your Excellency, if there's one other person in all of Iberia besides you who can read the sea chart and understand how to operate it, it can only be me.
Absurd. Even if you proved to me that you knew every grain of sand in Iberia, I would still not entrust this task to you.
Go. Don't add to your crimes.
I—
Return to your patrols. Remember: no unauthorized persons are to come near the central control room. It's the heart of the entire Port City.
Yes, ma'am!
Light up the sea chart... She has no idea what that point of light means, nor what the Inquisition will have to pay for it. Even I...
Who's there!
My apologies, Your Excellency. It's me.
Ugh—
Ngh—
*Iberian curse*... I only killed a roomful of Sea Terrors—the bodies weren't even ankle-deep. How did I end up so hurt I can't even pick up an apple...
Back in the day, I could've—tch.
NANDO!!!
Here, Instructor! What's wrong?
Nando, who taught you to cut apples into these cute little musbeast shapes that are so easy to pick up?
Reporting, Instructor, it was my sister! If you like them, she'll be happy too. Should I cut you some more?
And she never taught you that after cutting them so thoughtfully, you should at least put them somewhere the patient can reach?
Sorry, Instructor! I didn't realize you were hurt so badly you couldn't even sit up. I'll hand them right—
Let me.
Supervisor Clementia!
I won't interrupt your conversation. I'll head back to the checkpoint.
Visiting me in person? I heard an Islander turned himself in. You must be pretty busy right now.
The workshop you broke into belongs to the Bishop of the Deep, Aulus. He came to Iberia a hundred years ago, and he even helped design Rea-Iberia.
(Whistles) That's a big fish.
So why the long face?
The Islander problem is more serious than I thought, and Aulus's plan is anything but simple.
Speaking of which, I brought you a present.
A Seaborn corpse?
You can tell even when it's in pieces like this?
If you'd served in Ægir's Exercitus, you'd have picked up that skill too.
Little Helper, analyze the Seaborn's composition.
Scanning...

The matrix structure is entirely consistent with other Seaborn of the same type, but there are significant differences in the architecture of the nervous system. The logic of neural signal transmission is completely different from...
A new type of Seaborn...
Notice: the overall composition of this organism matches a previous identification record.
What? Little Helper, analyze and compare.
Analyzing... Related components were previously identified on Nacho.
Hey, mind translating what it's saying?
This is a new type of special Seaborn. Its underlying physiological mechanisms have been modified by someone. Nacho has been in contact with this special Seaborn, and...
Maybe I know what Aulus is really after.
Hey, young fella over there, care for some seaweed liquor?
We must keep ourselves pure. Drink corrupts a man. It—
Every day has its proper business. I reckon it's all to celebrate the Port City's Central District rising. Even the Penal Battalion over there just stopped by my stall.
...Fine, I'll have just a little. If I get blind drunk, I won't be able to make out the coordinates on the sea chart.
What do you need coordinates for at that point?! In two more hours, the Port City's Central District will rise right before your eyes!
Come and look—this is the sea chart that Ægir Supervisor left here. They say the Port City's coordinates are already on it.
The Central District... Can you imagine what that place looks like? What would it feel like to actually live there?
I heard some of the houses there have even the cracks between the bricks filled in with gold dust. Does that mean not a breath of wind gets in?
Can you imagine? A house the sea wind can't blow straight through?
...I grew up in a straw hut.
I never even imagined that one day I'd be looking at a sea chart connected to Ægir, searching it for names I'd only ever heard the old folks mention.
Those were all Iberia's cities once... Saints above, there really were that many.
Here, look, the Port City's coordinates are over there! It's still gray.
In two hours, it'll light up, right?
The shipyard workers must be busy tonight. I wonder which Iberian will get the honor of lighting up, with their own hands, a magnificent capital that's been silent for sixty-three years.
Probably some High Inquisitor Su Santidad trusts deeply. At this hour, they must already be getting ready.
Two hours to go. Everything's in place over at the cranes. How's the inspection on your boat coming along?
No problems! Just like High Inquisitor Fidela instructed, if the cranes break down, we've got a boat ready to head out and repair the equipment at any time!
