Then test the comms stability one more time. As soon as we give the signal, the operators at the Salvage Center will start the program and the salvage will officially begin.
Got it! Wait, we still haven't been given access to the comms system?
Access should've been granted half an hour ago. Go find High Inquisitor Fidela!
We're in. We just walked right in? This is the central control room for the entire Port City!
The floor, the walls... they can't really all be gold, can they? A furnace this huge—is it the Port City's power source? Come look, quick, and there's this too...
Valerio, what are you staring at that big black iron box for?
Navigation, power, communications—nearly every function of the Port City as a mobile city is kept running by whatever's inside this big iron box.
It looks like there's something moving in there—
Don't you touch it. High Inquisitor Fidela will have our heads.
Did that High Inquisitor tell you all this? What did you promise her to get her to let us in?
She turned me down without a shred of mercy before!
High Inquisitor Fidela must hold fast to her duties. Having her start up the sea chart system was a direct order from Lord Carmen.
Then how'd you pull it off this time? Tell me, quick! I talked myself hoarse and she acted like she didn't even hear me!
Return to your patrols. Remember: no unauthorized persons are to come near the central control room. It's the heart of the entire Port City.
Yes, ma'am!
Light up the sea chart... She has no idea what that point of light means, nor what the Inquisition will have to pay for it. Even I...
Who's there!
My apologies, Your Excellency. It's me.
Save it.
We've known each other no more than a week or two, and how many times have you pleaded on Estefanía's behalf? I should dismiss her and give us both some peace.
I understand. You must be tired of hearing me talk about her. So this time, I've come to tell you about myself.
You?
Before I met Tefi, I wandered all over Iberia as well. My wounds came from saving a friend, and in the salty sea wind, they were slow to heal.
The pain kept me from sleeping. On every curfew night, all I could do was think—think about how I'd fallen so low, think about everything in Iberia.
Until I met this Liberi singing shanties in a tavern. I could tell at a glance that she lived by deceiving people, but she bought me food with her own money.
After that, I wandered with her. She fooled many people with that noble act of hers, and she saved many people too.
She really seemed to think of herself as a noble of the Golden Age. She wanted to protect all her supporters, even to grant their wishes—mine included. That's why we came here.
And this time, the presumptuous request she made of you was only to save one more person.
...No wonder she let you come in with me. See? Even if she's stiff as a board, an honest story and real experience can still move her.
If you ask me, once we light up the coordinates and actually become proper "somebodies," we should write a book and tell everyone our story. I'll narrate, you write.
What's up? Why'd you go quiet? I still want to know which part of your past was so moving that it got through to that stone-faced High Inquisitor.
Is there any part of my past you don't already know?
Since Her Excellency the High Inquisitor has entrusted us with this great task, we mustn't waste a single second. Let's save the stories for when we get back, all right?
Ooh, sure, of course!
Still, shouldn't we confirm the procedure with High Inquisitor Fidela? Lighting up the sea chart is a really big deal...
Don't worry. High Inquisitor Fidela will be here soon.
Go on. As long as we can restore the sea chart system, everything will turn out the way you want.

The Islander who turned himself in wasn't lying. Over the past three days, we've confirmed the location of the attack suspects' hideout. To avoid tipping off the enemy, we haven't made any arrests yet.

Most of them are wounded and their morale is low, but their organizer is very cautious and didn't show himself until this morning. That's how we were able to confirm the hideout's location for certain.
Tonight, the Port City's Central District returns to Iberia's coastline, and those cultists who keep haunting us will face judgment.
Irene, does Su Santidad have any further instructions?
Lord Carmen won't take part in the arrests personally, but he gave clear instructions—
If the enemy are already captives of the abyss, their remains do not even deserve to be thrown into the sea. But if they are merely lost kin, then guide them ashore with the light.
Fall in! Move out!
Instructor!
I've plugged my ears. Go ahead.
You've only been resting for a few days! Your wounds are still seeping blood!
You want me to lie around in my messy, smelly room, watching you all march past my window to catch the mastermind I've been tracking all this time—
I'd get so mad my wounds would split open.
You're lying, Instructor.
If you're choosing to act when you have a perfectly good excuse to slack off, that means you think there's definitely something wrong with this mission.
Heh, sharp for once.
Is it... that serious?
I've got no proof. For now, just think of it as a wounded woman rambling from blood loss.
No matter how many Sea Terrors that Bishop can conjure up, he's only got one mouth to give people orders with. And for someone who has to hide in the shadows, that mouth isn't so convenient to use.
I don't believe he could pull all those strings by himself and direct those cultists and Islanders through such a precise attack plan.
You suspect he has someone helping him?
Here's hoping I'm overthinking it.
Keep yourself safe. Don't go dying on the biggest day Iberia's seen in decades.
Supervisor Clementia? You should be at the plaza for the celebration welcoming Rea-Iberia back. What are you doing here...
Aulus's plan is very likely still in motion. To keep anything else from going wrong, the Penal Battalion will begin making arrests tonight.
Tonight? Then my kin—
I've come to something of an understanding with Lord Iberia. All the Islanders will have the chance to leave here and go live in Ægir.
But not now.
Ægir has the right to relocate its kin, but not the right to interfere with tonight's arrests.
If these arrests and the trials that follow were derailed because of my interference, I can't be sure Iberia wouldn't descend into even greater unrest.
After your kin are arrested, they'll still have to spend some time with the Inquisition. But you can wait in Milliarium until your friends' trials are over.
...In Milliarium?
You've never directly caused any destruction or casualties, and you were only dragged into the attack against your will. Besides, your testimony was accurate and useful.
What Lord Iberia and I agreed on is that you can be the first Islander to move back to Ægir.
...Have I ever told you about this, Supervisor Clementia?
After the amputation, I was in a lot of pain, and very depressed. My reason told me my neighbor's revenge was understandable, but my feelings kept me from taking it out on Grandma.
So I did something Aquila and the others thought was really stupid—I tried to fit in with the Iberians, to prove to them that Islanders could get along with Iberians just fine.
I can recite every book of scripture, and I never missed a single service. Even though I could tell which neighbors had thrown the firebomb through our window, I'd still smile at them.
Until one day, the town's Calificador called on me to serve as deacon—
From what I understand, that's practically Iberia saying it accepts you.
It is. I was so happy I almost cried.

But I soon realized that the reason I was so happy wasn't because being a deacon was some great honor. It was just because most Islanders will never get that kind of "acceptance" in their whole lives. That's all it was.
I was ashamed of how happy I'd been.
There's nothing shameful about wanting a better life.
I know. But the fact that I can't go back to Ægir is already settled.
Nacho raised his right hand. The handiwork of a Golden Age artisan, including the bolt he'd lost and found again, moved as one, smooth and seamless.
But beneath the transparent casing, limbs that could only belong to a Seaborn twitched in hidden corners. They were what kept the prosthetic stable and eased its wearer's pain.
I underwent Mr. Aulus's surgery. If it weren't for that surgery, I couldn't have saved so many of my kin from the scene of the attack. I don't regret it.
Nacho...
I see. I'm withdrawing my proposal to move you back to Ægir ahead of the others.
But not because you underwent that surgery. It's because of the reason you chose to.
If the reason you accepted the surgery was to save more Islanders, then I imagine you'll need to do the same thing tonight.
Yes. Even with your guarantee, it's still an arrest operation. Tonight, someone's bound to resist, and someone's bound to get hurt.
I need to be there. I need to help.
Then I'll do everything I can to protect your right to move freely. Tonight, no one will be able to charge you with a crime because of those Seaborn limbs.
And when the moment comes that you're truly assimilated by the Seaborn, I'll set you free with my own hands.
How are things?
The Iberians are all gathered in the plaza. We've still got too many wounded—there's no way to organize anything...
The Mentor will help us.
Is Mr. Aulus still in the workshop?
Yeah.
I really don't know how he's going to carry out the next part of the plan...

Wait, footsteps—
Ugh...
Block cleared, sir. This Aulus the Islander just mentioned, is he...
The Bishop of the Deep we're looking for.
Advance! Surround that workshop!
This point is the Port City, right? Your hometown. It's just still dark for now.
Every gray coordinate is a town sleeping beneath the sea. Just how much Iberia has lost... it's plain to see.
I never lived through that era, so honestly, I can't imagine how much you miss this place. But when I think that we're about to haul it up with our own hands—I can't stop shaking all over.
Be honest—was this moment the whole reason you got me to work at the shipyard?
If you're homesick, just say so! You're my number-one supporter, and you've gotten me out of plenty of jams along the way. Of course I'll help you!
You've already helped me a great deal, Lady de Toledo. This really is something I could never have done on my own.
In these past few decades, Iberia has changed too much. Half of what once existed has already been forgotten, and the other half has either changed its shape or its name.
If not for landmarks like Aarón, whose name and location never changed, to use as reference points, we couldn't even begin to match today's maps to those of the past.
To restore the sea chart system, the operator needs to know every inch of Iberia, untangle the jumbled geographical data, and match every coordinate of the past to the present, one by one.
I can do it. Look, I'm already doing it!
It's been ten years since the first time I lied to a Calificador back in my little hometown. Ten years I've been a con artist, just to scrape by and have a roof over my head.
Honestly, a few times I could tell the other person knew perfectly well I was just some lowlife up to no good, but they were still willing to keep "believing" in me.
They'd play along with my "de Toledo" act, and they'd tell me lots of their own stories too—about their hometowns already sunk beneath the sea, their families with not even bones left behind.

I never really understood why they were willing to believe in me. All I could do was share more of what I'd conned out of people with them, and now and then use some not-so-honorable tricks to solve their little problems.
But since coming to the Port City... more and more people believe in me, and I can do less and less for each of them.
So that day, when you told me I should become a real "somebody," my only regret was that you didn't say it sooner. That's the only way I can do more for people who've lost their way.
It's not too late, Lady de Toledo. So long as you have the perseverance and the courage to bear that responsibility.
Responsibility?
I told you the burn scars on my body came from helping a friend.
Yeah. They look really painful. You still can't sleep through the night.
I helped that friend become what you call a "somebody." But sadly, he ruined everything we'd built together. He didn't see the job through properly.
Because he didn't take responsibility?
Because he didn't have the courage to finish what he'd started.
And you, Lady de Toledo?
Hey, don't you know me by now?!
That's precisely because I know you too well.
Huh?
You're a con artist, and lies always have a beginning but never an end.
Of course, you're also very gifted. Your memory is astonishing, and no one knows Iberia better than you do. Thanks to you, the sea chart system is now fully restored.
You've made a fine beginning, and I can see it through to the end for you—
By erasing Rea-Iberia's coordinates from history entirely.
I don't understand... Valerio, why? If I messed something up, we can ask High Inquisitor Fidela to figure something out. Didn't you say she'd be here soon—
Fidela isn't coming.

The man entered a string of passcodes into the interface of the sea chart system Tefi had started up. An ominous premonition welled up in Tefi's heart. She wanted to stop him, but it was already too late.
The man moved his finger to Rea-Iberia's gray coordinate point and pressed down.
You're still using your own misfortunes to plead on her behalf.
No. What I mean to say is that the girl has helped many people, but in the end she's still a child, and a con artist.
That Iberia's duties have fallen onto the shoulders of a swindler proves how degenerate this nation has become.
Describing Iberia as "degenerate" alone is enough to have you thrown in a cell.
But the High Inquisitor who was moved by my words only a few days ago now finds this sort of story not so moving after all, doesn't she?
Nearly every night, you're nowhere to be seen in the shipyard. And at the same time, the Islanders who carry an air of danger about them have been quietly disappearing...
Do you enjoy playing two entirely different roles?
Silence!
It seems if I keep talking, you won't give me a chance to open my mouth at all.
Precisely because you're still able to open your mouth, I'll grant you a little respect—you dodged a High Inquisitor's sword, sophist.
Who are you? What is it you really want with me? If I took off one of your arms, would human blood flow out, or the revolting slime of a Sea Terror?
Mind your tongue, young one.
Besides, the only thing in this entire shipyard that would revolt you was delivered into your hands just a few days ago.
What are you saying...
You didn't know?
Hahaha, Carmen is truly far too considerate of his student.

Then I suppose you also don't know that the "key" to restarting Rea-Iberia—the "hope" that will return the land beneath our feet to the Golden Age—was bought with everything the Inquisition has ever been.
No! Su Santidad would never hide something so important from me.
Did he deliberately hide it, or did you deliberately not listen?
How could I deliberately... Could it be that the day Su Santidad summoned me to the Inquisition's temporary headquarters, he meant to tell me all of this...
And where were you then?
You made your choice long ago. You were afraid of the thriving scenes in the city, because you know Iberia's chronic ills are just like the wounds on your body—they won't heal easily in the sea wind.
All those optimistic words were nothing but a way of deceiving yourself.
And sadder still, when you open that iron box and face everything the Inquisition has been, you'll find you cannot accept the truth it holds.
You are not a fit High Inquisitor, Fidela. Look at your lantern. The flame is flickering.

You're exhausted, aren't you? Facing the conflict between the Islanders and the Iberian people, facing Sea Terrors you can never finish killing, facing a self that longs for the future yet is sickened by the present.

You don't let the Penal Battalion soldiers under you interrogate the Islanders and the cultists because you don't want them tainted by the same vices as you, don't want them wavering in their faith in the Inquisition too. Isn't that so?

But if Iberia hadn't given people pointless hope, you would never have had to bear all this. You've long grown used to enduring the pain of your wounds, but you're not good at praying for them to heal.
Who are you, really? How do you know so much about me, and about the Inquisition?!
Even now, you still care about the Inquisition's safety. It's like seeing my former self... But he's already dead.
Dead?
Fidela wanted to press further, but the next second she saw the scars beneath Valerio's cloak, spreading from his back all the way to his cheek.
And at his waist was a weapon Fidela knew all too well—an Inquisition handcannon, bearing engravings that belonged to a Saint alone.

Not long after Fidela became Carmen's student, she heard that two Saints had fought the Seaborn in a great fire until their last breath, leaving not even their bones behind. Carmen said they died for the future of Iberia.
When she saw Dario off, she had silently recited those two great names before his grave. And the Saint who had been the more skilled with a handcannon was none other than—
Saint Valerio... How can this be...
I, too, wished to die in that great fire, to die in the inscription on a stone tablet. But I must correct Iberia's mistake.
And you know what that mistake is.
Our land is still rife with evil... Even within the Inquisition, it is no pure sanctuary.
Saint Valerio, I want to root it all out. When the sun rises again tomorrow, I hope what it shines upon... is a pure Iberia, a nation to be proud of.
That's why I've given everything I have to carry out judgment alone, hoping to keep the soldiers under me far from the shadow of war, to let them escape the cycle of hatred.
After Aquila died, I went through the Inquisition's records again—as I do after every interrogation or execution of Islanders and Church of the Deep cultists.
I'm afraid I've made the wrong decisions and betrayed the virtues the Saints taught us. But...
Four times. In my twenty years as High Inquisitor, among tens of thousands of suspects, I remember clearly that I made four mistakes.
I cannot greet Iberia's tomorrow with a clear conscience. Its light will not shine upon me...
You've done well enough, High Inquisitor. The root of it all is that Iberia's dawn should never have come so soon.
You have plans of your own.
I told you, I came to correct a mistake.
High Inquisitor, your light is about to go out.
I can light it again, with the conviction of a Saint returned from the dead.
...What do you need me to do?
On the night of the salvage celebration, leave this place.
The sound of celebration drifted from the distant plaza, while well-trained Penal Battalion soldiers, cloaked in the night, purged sin.
The shipwrights bustled about the docks. They didn't dare set foot fully into the pitch-black sea, but their eyes shone with curiosity.
Fidela looked at the lantern in her hand. The light in the sea wind was tinged the color of blood. Apart from the moonlight, it was the only source of light on the entire shore.
It struggled weakly. It was close to going out.
Have I had too much to drink? Why are all those Inquisitors and Penal Battalion soldiers suddenly running?
Did they move the salvage up? Stop pushing, let me have a look too—
On the sea chart... the coordinates are gone...
What?
The sea chart! The coordinates for the Port City are gone, I can't see them!
The golden sea chart was still projected in the sky above the plaza, but within it, one unremarkable gray point of light had quietly vanished.
Vanishing along with it was the glow of the Port City's dozens of lighthouses.
More and more people raised their heads. In vain they searched for the coordinates, for the very reason they'd gathered in the plaza to celebrate, and found nothing.
The sea chart had lost all meaning to the Iberians. It was as if Rea-Iberia would never light up again, would never... come back.
You erased Rea-Iberia's coordinates? Why... Valerio, why would you do this!
You still don't understand. For you, and for me, getting into the central control room was always part of the plan—the most important part.
You... lied to me?
Now you've become a "somebody" too, I suppose... just not the one who lit up the sea chart.
You!
Our journey ends here, Tefi.
The Penal Battalion should seal this place off soon. I still have to go see a very important friend.
Cheer up. Or sing a song.
At least you didn't let this "supporter" of yours down, did you?
North side door? The two basement entrances on the south side?
All sealed!
Good. Move in!
...No one's here?
Seaborn! Everyone, on guard!
Penal Battalion, eyes front! Eliminate the Seaborn threat first!
Aulus isn't here, and the number of Islanders who took part in the attack doesn't match our estimate... No, where did they go?
Penal Battalion, Inquisitors, all Iberians, listen well—
Penal Battalion, Inquisitors, all Iberians, listen well—
The Port City's Central District has already left the salvage zone and is now heading for the open sea.
The Port City's coordinates—its identification—have been completely erased. It no longer exists on either Iberia's or Ægir's sea charts.

The positioning and navigation functions of every lighthouse have been disabled as well. Don't even bother trying to repair them. Every piece of technology in those lighthouses is ours—the Islanders'.
In your arrogance, you thought that attack was only meant to damage the Port City. But the Port City never belonged to you alone. Iberia never belonged to you alone.
Recognize all Islanders as lawful citizens. Make public every case file concerning Islanders from the past several decades, and formally apologize for every wrongful conviction among them.
Do that, and then we'll talk about what becomes of the Port City.

lines.st: Beyond the glass curtain wall lies murky, dark seawater.

There should have been a semaphore tower there, hung thick with flags. In this capital where ten thousand sails came to call, the only language shared by every merchant and envoy was the signals that tower flew.
But now, it has vanished without a trace.

lines.x: If you insist on treating this as repayment of your debt to me, then consider it paid in full, Valerio.
Thanks to you erasing the Port City's coordinates and blinding the Inquisition...
It can finally resume the journey it put off for more than sixty years.
It's been a long time indeed, Rea-Iberia.
Supervisor Clementia!
Tacita, what's the situation at the Salvage Center?
All access to the Salvage Center has been locked. None of the staff can get in.
The lockdown wasn't done through the system Ægir designed for the Salvage Center. It used an older, more fundamental command—one perhaps only the Port City's designer would know to use.
Aulus...
Before the lighthouse attack, I left a backdoor in the system. I might be able to overwrite the command, restore access, and lift the lockdown on the Salvage Center.

I'll head to the Salvage Center right away, but things on shore aren't looking good either. The Inquisition's operation to arrest the Islanders is bound to have run into trouble, and Nacho's already gone to find his scattered kin. You—
I'll go and calm our kin as well.
It seems sitting in on the interrogation helped you reach a conclusion.
Actually, not yet... But if I understand correctly, the Islanders in the Mutual Aid Society never all wanted the same thing to begin with.
Even if they're holding the Port City's Central District hostage now, would recognition as citizens and a public apology for wrongful convictions really satisfy every Islander?
In Ægir's general education, the Islanders are treated as a single group. Perhaps that's how Iberia sees them too.
But I've met Aquila. I've met Nacho. Even though I only know a few dozen Islanders from the Salvage Center, I understand that each of them is different, and each of them has their own choices.
I can't commit myself to helping them the way you have, but I have my own questions to work through.
And who knows—this way, I might be able to learn something from them about where the Central District has gone.
I look forward to hearing your conclusion, Tacita. Go on.
Yes, ma'am!
*Iberian curse*, there's no end to them...
You, over there! Don't just stand there gawking!
Captain, I can't swing my halberd anymore...
They just keep crawling out of the cracks in the district! We need the Inquisitors' lights!
I can't even see what's under my feet right now. I can't tell if I'm stepping on a Sea Terror's tentacle or...
Get a grip, soldier!
Irene, thank you...
Look at the Sea Terrors, not at the lanterns in my hand or the Inquisitors'. Staring at the light will only make it harder and harder for you to adjust to the dark.
Ten seconds. Look into this darkness for ten seconds. Trust me, you won't become these abominations' target.

...Three, two, one...
I-I can see!
Wow, so many Sea Terror corpses... Did you do all of...
Congratulations on adjusting to the dark, soldier. Your comrades can easily protect you for a mere ten seconds. Trust in us.
Now it's your turn to do the same for others.
Understood!
...The whole way out of the shipyard, it's been Sea Terrors everywhere...
What have I helped Valerio do... All I wanted was to light up the Port City's coordinates, to get Salvador to believe in me, I...
How did I end up here...
She knew the plaza before her all too well.

Two weeks ago, she had just arrived in the Port City's Outer District. She'd thrown an arm around a statue of someone she didn't even know and, just like always, tricked her supporters into trusting her, earning herself a night's lodging and a few square meals.

She had thought she and Valerio were the perfect partners. He knew so much from before the Profound Silence, he would patch the holes in her stories, and he would rein her in whenever she went too far.
She had thought Valerio was simply homesick. That was why he'd suggested coming to the Port City, why he'd had her sing that banned shanty again and again, wearing a look of longing.
Today a ship sets sail...♪
Past the lighthouse... past... the church...♪
...mist... drifts to the shore...♪
Raise the sails... raise the sails...♪
The helm's not in the wind's hands♪
Valerio! No, you're—
Su Santidad... What are you doing here?!
I knew you were in the Outer District, but this is the first time I've seen you since the launch ceremony—of course! As an upstanding citizen, I shouldn't be seeing you at all...
My presence here means something has already gone wrong.
Gone wrong? You don't mean the shipyard's...
I know you.
At the salvage launch ceremony two weeks ago, you led the singing of this shanty. A century ago, its author did the very same thing in this very plaza.
Ever since, whenever a ship set sail, the Iberians on the docks would sing this song on the shore. A late colleague of mine was very fond of it.
Su Santidad...
I salute your singing, young one. That song is a piece of Iberia's history—undeniable, and yet fading away.
Tell me, what do you see happening in Iberia now?
A disaster...
Compared to sixty-three years ago, it is nothing worth mentioning.
But fear isn't something you can compare!
Sea Terrors are crawling onto the streets, the Port City's coordinates have vanished, and the one behind all of this is... is...
(Takes a deep breath)
Su Santidad, I-I was already planning to turn myself in to the Inquisition! I'm the one who restored the sea chart system, and I'm the one who watched the Port City's coordinates disappear!
Become a "somebody"... How could I have believed him so easily...
I've always lived by conning people. Even what I'm telling you right now—I can't tell whether it's a heartfelt confession or an excuse to win your sympathy. I—
All you need to tell me is who your companion is.
Y-you believe me?
One who doubts even herself can no longer deceive others.
Where did the two of you meet?
At a little tavern in Finridge.
I was singing a hazy, patchy version of the shanty back then, trying to get a bit of money for lodging out of the customers. Everyone left except him. He looked so pitiful that I bought him a meal.
