Aquila, Gaius, Breogan. Dario, Alfonso. Tullia, Ulpianus. Every person this war has cast aside should have become a possibility for the future.
For those who've already died or disappeared without a trace, there's nothing I can do. But many who've been cast aside are still struggling.
Ángela, Soledad, Drusa, Nacho—and you, Aulus. Every one of you still has the chance to become a possibility for the future.
But none of you is more important, or more deserving of life, than any other.

How many people have you already selfishly sacrificed? How many precious possibilities have you snuffed out? That you still have a chance to realize your ideals at all is the greatest injustice in this world.
So, what else would you like to choose?
Now, as a "down payment"—
It's time you told me where the Port City's Central District has gone.
I found you, and you are not surprised.
You weren't surprised that I came back from the dead either, Su Santidad.

With Rea-Iberia's coordinates permanently gone from the sea chart, the Penal Battalion and the Inquisitors would focus first on guarding against Seaborn coming ashore, and the new Supervisor would surely go to check on the Salvage Center.

And your pride and arrogance would drive you to find the true culprit who erased the coordinates first—the one who saw through your careful arrangements, who shook your loyal student, who knows the Inquisition, and you, very well.
But apart from Fidela, no one should have known that Tefi and I entered the central control room. How did you narrow your suspicions down to us?
In the checkpoint's records, I found that an upright Penal Battalion recruit had stopped an unidentified musician before the salvage launch ceremony began.
Later, he saw her gathering a crowd and giving a speech at the shipyard—on the very day the Islander Aquila seized her chance to act and was arrested.
It seems I was a little short on luck.

You assisted the Bishop of the Deep. First, you diverted the Inquisition's attention with the attack on the lighthouses. Then, on the day of the celebration, you erased Rea-Iberia's coordinates so the Inquisition could not track the Central District.
Do you seek revenge on me, on the Inquisition? Because of that great fire fifty-three years ago?
Revenge... No.
Aulus and I have never walked the same path. He gave me a second life, and I didn't want to be in his debt. But I have another purpose.
The former Saint turned his back on his colleague. It was the trust that still remained between them after more than fifty years apart.
He took a rapier from the weapon rack. There was no name engraved on it; it belonged to no one. The lives devoted to Iberia were always so brief. They could not even leave behind a name.
With lowered eyes, he carefully wiped the weapon in his hands. A cold flame burned fiercely within his chest, melting away the rust and dust from the blade.
In these fifty-odd years, I've walked through much of Iberia—famine, plague, unrest, crime... I've come to be ashamed of the pride I once had.
And you—while Iberia is still barely clinging to life, you want to take yet another step forward?
Rea-Iberia was always a part of this land. Sooner or later, it must return to our coastline.
But why now?
In Sal Viento, numbed people took a Bishop of the Deep as their only salvation. Even with the Inquisition's intervention, they're still in a sorry state.
In Gran Faro, the Stultifera Navis, that symbol of glory, sank into the sea. The ark of the Golden Age is gone without a trace.
Tefi, that naive swindler. She can win followers with a single tune, a single story. Foolish commoners deceive one another and reap an imaginary future without any effort at all.
Countless Iberians need the guidance of a Saint, countless corrupted virtues need correcting—and I'm doing what you should have done yourself.
Doesn't all of this show that Iberia is still in dire straits? Doesn't it show that we should keep to our original course, to keep a crumbling Iberia alive?
Valerio, have you ever considered what price we would pay for continuing to enforce the old ways of governance upon this fragile land?
To maintain Iberia's order, we have already paid an enormous price.

We built the foundation of the Inquisitors' Arts on abominations. We gave the lives of countless colleagues to win the common folk the right to live by the sea. We treated everything from the ocean as our enemy.
Nothing that was sacrificed will ever come back.
And I was once a part of that too.
Valerio...
I won't lie to you, Carmen. I once thought of taking revenge on you.
When that traitor spat on everything the Inquisition had given and worshiped the heretical sea god amid the burning Seaborn, I hated you—how dare you believe I'd ever side with the likes of him.
But I was glad too. If you were willing to bear the price of abandoning a companion, then you could surely lead Iberia further.
It was never the great fire that I held against you, Carmen.

What I held against you was these fifty-odd years—dragging this undying body around, watching Iberia go from bad to worse, watching sin and evil sprout from rotting morals, and being powerless to do anything about it.
That half-dead body of yours has made you too impatient. You were never powerless.
That's right. When you announced the Salvage Plan, I realized I wasn't powerless. If I believe Iberia's steward is wrong, then I should correct it.
Carmen, if you're too cowardly to keep guiding Iberia, I'll take your place.
I will become Iberia's new Pope.
Alchemical symbols flickered across Valerio's body. Blue points of light erupted with scorching heat.
The alchemical formulae within this body seemed to be resonating, from afar, with the formulae engraved on another body, somewhere else.
A human body and a Seaborn body burned together in this moment, just as they had more than fifty years before.
Valerio, what are you doing!

Whatever Aulus and the Islanders want to do with the Port City's Central District has nothing to do with my Iberia. All I know is that an old capital gilded with gold dust is the last thing Iberia needs right now.
Then let the capital of the Golden Age sink to the bottom of the sea forever.
Still no move from the Inquisition since we put out our demands?
None... They seem to be evacuating the civilians first, and our innocent Islander kin too.
The streets are crawling with Sea Terrors now, and some of them are our...
Don't think about that!
Gaius and the others made their choice. So did we.
F... Found you...
Nacho? What are you doing here?
I heard the broadcast. So taking the Port City's Central District hostage to negotiate was your goal all along. Whatever it is you're trying to do—
Wait, why are there only this many of you?
A few days ago, after you left the workshop, some of our kin left too.
They couldn't accept Gaius turning into that kind of monster. All they wanted was to fight for a bit more food, or to get harassed a little less by the Iberians.
But we want real guarantees.
The Mentor promised us he'd move the Port City's Central District somewhere nobody knows. It's our only bargaining chip.
Only Mr. Aulus knows? Then how can you be sure the negotiations will go well...
Right—are any of our kin at the shipyard?
We didn't send anyone to the shipyard.
It wasn't you who erased the Port City's coordinates?
We don't know much either. Just that the Mentor seems to have a collaborator.
A collaborator... Then where is he?
We've never seen him. He—

What's going on? The tremors are coming from the direction of the shipyard...
No, from the sea too?
*cough cough* The explosion came from the central control room! I'll go—
Don't go in there!
Irene?
Su Santidad once entrusted me with delivering the "key" that keeps all of the Port City's functions running to the shipyard. I'll take full responsibility for dealing with what comes next.
Return to your post.
Yes, ma'am.
Smoke billowed up, and Irene couldn't make out what was happening in the central control room. But she could clearly hear where the sound of seawater boiling away was coming from—
The iron box holding the Seaborn—!
There are scorch marks from alchemy on it... No!
The main engine's operating light has gone out. The Central District of Rea-Iberia... has sunk back into the sea?
The explosion...
So this was Lord Valerio's plan. Not until virtue returns to the Iberian people should that capital rise...
I was wondering why someone in a High Inquisitor's uniform was loitering by the sea instead of rushing to the shipyard. Who'd have guessed it was one of the bombers?
Hm, but your voice sounds kind of familiar. A few days ago, when I got ambushed at the workshop and called for backup, this was the voice that left me to a swarm of Sea Terrors.
Though back then, you sounded a lot more sure of yourself.
You're... the Penal Battalion instructor?
You know me?
There are precious few Islanders connected to the Penal Battalion. I've heard your story.
I also know how you were treated at the training grounds.
What, you want to apologize on behalf of the people who bullied me?
You don't look like you need that. Besides, after tonight, evil both inside and outside the Inquisition will be dealt with far more strictly. No one will do such things again.
The Iberia you're imagining sounds even more boring than the original.
Boring... You call a pure, virtuous nation boring?
If what you mean is a nation where no one's allowed to make mistakes, and no one ever makes one again—yeah.
Lots of people know I got treated badly at the training grounds, but not many know what actually happened.
My first night there, a Liberi two heads taller than me hauled me out of bed and beat me up, trying to run me out of the place.
Half a month later, I knocked him flat in close-quarters combat class. Beat him so badly he couldn't show his face for a week.

Later he apologized. Back in his hometown, a Church of the Deep cultist had deliberately signed up for training just to carry out a suicide attack. He was afraid I was the same kind of person. But obviously, time proved everything.
We were good friends ever since, right up until he died on a mission half a year ago.
Even if the two of you buried the hatchet, it doesn't mean what he did before was right.
Right. But I never forgave him either. Every time we drank seaweed liquor together, I made him pay.
What kind of...
I really hate arguing from experience, but you seem older than me, and you've definitely seen a lot more Iberians than I have.
I can't tell if you've just been sitting in judgment for too long, or if you've spent more time facing Seaborn than actual people.
You don't seem to realize that in Iberia, there's really only one reason people make mistakes—they want a better life.
Islanders join the Church of the Deep just to be called "kin," a High Inquisitor acts harshly to eliminate threats... Everyone's making mistakes.
You probably know that too. That's why you're out here by the sea catching the breeze with that sour look on your face, with the lantern in your hand flickering on and off.
I know I'm guilty. I won't make excuses for myself.
But if austerity can buy Iberia lasting prosperity, isn't it worth it?
It isn't.
Because after all the boring stuff we've talked about here, I've only picked up one thing: you're disappointed in yourself, and you've never accepted that you make mistakes.
But if you don't accept it, how are you supposed to atone to the Islanders who were really affected by you, by the Inquisition?
Or maybe I'll make you atone tonight.
What do you mean?
The black-haired Ægir drew the sword from her hip. Compared to the High Inquisitor's rapier, it was far too fierce and strange, yet it lay obediently in the Ægir's hand like a silver chain.
As a genuine Islander, I figure I can demand some answers from you on behalf of my kin.
What are you doing!
Not bad, you've still got survival instincts. Guess we can still talk.

I've been an instructor at the Inquisition's training grounds for ten years. I've seen thousands upon thousands of Penal Battalion recruits. They cry, they get scared, they hate, they make mistakes—and I only know one way to teach them.
With my sword.
The explosion came from the shipyard... When you erased the Port City's coordinates for Aulus, you had already made preparations for your own plan.
Yes. Even if that Bishop of the Deep's plan failed, I couldn't allow Iberia to recover this capital so steeped in sin.
It would drag Iberians, whose souls and virtue are already overburdened, into an even deeper mire.
Virtue... overburdened...
Valerio, in the fifty-odd years since you were reborn, facing countless suffering Iberians—this is the conclusion you've reached?
Then I regret to say your resurrection was indeed a mistake.
What?
You've been to Sal Viento.
Ignorant, numbed residents, utterly unaware of their own degeneration.
Since you saw the Bishop of the Deep Quintus, you must also know that he fancied himself the protector of the faithful there, trading the sacrifice of individuals for the bread of the many.
Does that approach not seem familiar to you?
Carmen, how dare you!
When Dario reported to me, I felt no relief that the Church of the Deep had lost a Bishop for good. Instead, I felt sorrow.
The people of Sal Viento were undoubtedly grateful to Quintus. In a corner the Inquisition had abandoned, another faith—strange and evil—kept them alive.
But how could merely staying alive ever be enough?
Even that girl named Anita was moved by a melody from Ægir, and wished to leave Sal Viento, where at least she could scrape by.
And our people, in the sixty-three years since the Profound Silence, have clung to life on this barren land cut off from the world. How are they to endure?
The Inquisition's light will illuminate the holy path. The people of Iberia need only follow.
How can land that cannot grow crops make people stay? How can a bitter, dried-up well not make them despair? No holy light can hide the fact that the granaries are empty.
You condemn the degeneration of today's Iberians, yet have you never considered how easily virtue crumbles when faced with the despair of mere survival?
But without virtue, the Iberian people would cease to exist!
If not for the Inquisition's scriptures, Iberians would have lost all dignity as human beings after the Profound Silence. What would it matter, then, even if we reclaimed our lost lands?
Matter?
Our late friend Alfonso has already shown us what reclaiming our lands means.
What happened on the Stultifera Navis would be torture for anyone. He held on with everything he had aboard that great ship of the Golden Age. Why?
A sliver of hope, a sliver of longing—stronger than all doctrine and discipline.
The workers of Gran Faro who stood fast beneath the dimmed Eye of Iberia—what they held in their hearts must have been the glory of the Golden Age as well.
Even you—you understand this too.
Me?
You claim you traveled with Estefanía to correct her wrongdoing, and to use her knowledge of Iberia's geography to achieve your own ends.
That's right.
But before our reunion, I met that girl in the plaza. She told me how the two of you met.
That banned shanty is a relic of the Golden Age, and it was once the song you loved most.
If you had no longing for Iberia's glorious past, you would never have given Estefanía a second glance in that tavern in Finridge. Is that not so?
Now Ægir's fleet is stationed in Iberia's coastal waters. On the matter of the Seaborn, we have finally been given a chance to breathe.
As you said, I am arrogant, Valerio.
The one future I have never imagined is one in which Iberia cannot regain its glory.
Glory. Easier said than done...
Indeed. But at the very least, we must not cling to the Inquisition's past achievements and strangle Iberia's possibilities.
So you deliberately relaxed the restrictions on the Islanders?
The conflict between the Islanders and the Iberians is the first problem that must be solved. We still have a long road ahead.
Some of them will be formally recognized as citizens of Iberia, and where the rest will go... is one of the reasons I chose to cooperate with Ægir.
Rea-Iberia will bear witness to the reconciliation of the Islanders and the Iberians, and it will be Iberia's opportunity to lift its isolation.

The Inquisition's role is going to change drastically. And you put the Seaborn we rescued from the Port City back into its original cage. The core of the Arts that sustains the Inquisition's lights is weakening.
Our soldiers possess an unrivaled will. One day the lights will go out, but they will kindle the sparks in their lanterns once more with their own hearts.
Then from now on, the problems Iberia faces won't just be the ones the sea brings.

And you and I both know that whether it's the conflict between the Islanders and the Iberians, the transformation of the Inquisition, or other nations' curiosity about Iberia once the isolation is lifted—every one of them is a risk.
You can't possibly have a foolproof plan right now.
No. Since we founded the Inquisition together, when have we ever had a foolproof plan?
But we do share one understanding—if you believe your insight, ability, and resolve far surpass mine, you will always have the chance to topple me, step over me, kill me.
It's for this very moment that I've come before you.
Valerio took up the freshly tended rapier. At his waist, the handcannon bearing a Saint's engravings came into view.
Carmen I Iberia, on behalf of all that the Inquisition once was, to defend Iberia's purity and virtue, I challenge you to a duel.
Your answer?
I accept your challenge, Valerio.
...Do you hear that? That's not cannon fire from the defense line.
It's coming from the direction of the coast.
...Supervisor... let me... let me in...
No time... I'll die...
So you've come after all, Nacho.
The Port City's Central District... sank?
That's what those Penal Battalion soldiers were shouting as they ran for the shore.
But the Port City's Central District is our only bargaining chip in these negotiations...
Not anymore. We hijacked the Port City's Central District, and now it's been blown up and sunk who knows where. Who do you think it's going to look like did it?
The charges against the Islanders will only get heavier.

The cooperation between Ægir and Iberia was held together by the Port City Salvage Plan in the first place. If the Port City's Central District is gone for good... I'm afraid not even Supervisor Clementia will be able to help us.
But we didn't do it, it couldn't have been us... I wanted to see that aqueduct my father went on about his whole life. How could I ever blow up the Port City's Central District...
When Gaius said he'd sink the Port City's Central District to the bottom of the sea forever, you didn't stop him either, did you?
I thought he was just talking out of anger! Besides, he's already...
Shut up. None of you have the right to talk about him. At least he actually did something. If anyone still wants to do something, come with me.
It's too late now for proving anything, for innocence or guilt. We go kill the ones who deserve it, and then we leave this place.
She's lost her mind...
But she's not wrong. Everyone's got to find their own way out.
Earlier, some little Ægir girl came to find me and asked if I wanted to go with her. She said something about choices—I didn't get it.
I said no, but she kept following me, telling me to think it over. Now I guess I'd better go find her. Maybe she can save my life.
Don't just stand there either, Nacho. Before the Penal Battalion comes to arrest you—
I'm going to find the Port City's Central District.
And then beg for forgiveness?
No.
Most of us never really wanted to destroy the Port City's Central District.
It's true that plenty of people have destroyed what they made with their own hands. But the Port City's Central District... too many people poured their hearts into it.
Besides, we all still want to see what the Central District looks like, don't we?
We... do...
No matter when, if we care about it, then we go and find it.
Lots of people here care about it. Whether they're Penal Battalion or ordinary folks, if they care, their first instinct should be the same as ours—to go find it.
If none of us is there when that happens, that's when we'll truly be branded with a crime we can never wash away.
Even now, you're still dreaming you can make peace with those people... even work with them?
I know it's already too late, but it's not impossible. At least, if we can just recover the Port City's Central District...
Recover the Port City's Central District... You make it sound so easy. It's sunk somewhere in a sea teeming with Sea Terrors, and nobody knows where. You think you can find it?
...If Aquila could find one tiny bolt in the sea.
That was close to shore! How far away is the Port City's Central District, and how far can you swim? One kilometer, two? And then what—who's going to go collect your body?
Nacho silently studied his prosthetic.
The same way I saved all of you on the day of the lighthouse attack—that's how I'll find the Port City's Central District now.
If I really do find where it is, would you be willing to help me bring it back?
...I'll think about it.
But that's our choice to make now.
Aulus, at the speed the Port City's Central District was traveling... could it be close to its destination by now?
Not a chance. What's worse, the Port City's Central District has a very complete power system. The main engine failing isn't enough to make it sink on the spot.
For now it'll only drift off course. But without anyone intervening, it will eventually sink... As for where, even I can't calculate that.
If I were truly willing to cooperate with you, I'd have other ways of locating it, of course. A city doesn't just vanish into thin air.
Once the drone arrays are repaired, Ægir's technology could do the same. But the problem has always been—time.
Regrettably, I really don't have Mártus's talents.
I'm nowhere near Seaborn enough to hear the voice of every Seaborn in the sea. Otherwise, I could never be standing here speaking to you with a clear head.
We can't wait that long. The Islanders' situation is getting worse every second.
I didn't come here to ask you for help. I just need Mr. Aulus to tell me one thing.
These Seaborn limbs on my arm... how do I make them start assimilating me again?
Nacho, you must understand what that would mean.

Yes. Mr. Aulus, you said it yourself just now. If the degree of Seaborn transformation is high enough, you can hear more of the Seaborn's voices. One of them is bound to know where the Central District went.
By then, I probably won't be able to speak anymore. But we can agree on a way to communicate—I could sign numbers with my hands, or some other movement a Seaborn can manage.
Before I completely forget who I am, I should have enough time to tell you the coordinates of the Port City's Central District.
Only, after that... Supervisor Clementia, please kill me.
I really don't want to...
I understand.
The last thing Nacho saw was the tip of Clementia's sword sweeping past Aulus's eyes and pointing at him.
And Aulus, too, drew his sword, and leveled it straight at Clementia.
Nacho closed his eyes, unwilling to think any more about what that meant. From here on, there was only one thing left for him to do.
The smell of blood, both familiar and unfamiliar, flooded into Nacho's nose.
Blood kept seeping from Clementia's sword hand. On the other side, Aulus bore an even more ghastly wound.

Tiny, deep-blue limbs reached out from the depths of the wound, hooking onto the skin, trying to close the gash in his flesh. But before they could even begin to grow, they withered and died one after another.
So the negotiations have completely broken down, have they?
All that's changed is that you no longer need to hand back the Port City's Central District, Aulus.
...Nacho shouldn't die here.
No one is going to die here.
Nacho, look at your prosthetic.
...Supervisor Clementia?
Those Seaborn limbs... You cut them all off? Why?
There's another way. A way that doesn't need a sacrifice.
But that's no longer any concern of yours, Aulus. Take your wound and go. It won't kill you, but it will never heal either.
That sword—it uses Class IV weapon technology?
With a few improvements.
Class IV weapons were designed based on biological information to begin with, so naturally they can be used to transmit information as well.
What I need from you will be conveyed through special neural signals released by that wound. Your brain will be the only receiving terminal.
And if you fail to hold up your end, I can carry out your overdue execution at any time.
So in the end, my life is still in your hands?
As it should have been from the start.
Heh.
...I hope you'll keep your promise too.
Nacho.
Supervisor Clementia, your wounds...
I'm all right.
Clementia bent down and picked up a tiny part from among the severed Seaborn limbs.
Here, take this. Hold on to it.
The bolt... It's this bolt again. Why?
Why... What am I supposed to remember? What am I supposed to do?
First it was Grandma Rufina. In those last few years, I brought her water, cooked her porridge, changed her dressings every day. I thought she'd get better... But she didn't. Nothing changed.
She died, and she left this bolt to me.
Then it was Aquila. I tried going to the Inquisition myself, and I tried begging Mr. Aulus and the other Islanders in the Mutual Aid Society for help... But still nothing changed.
She died too, and all she left me was this bolt, again.
This time, I didn't care if I turned into a Seaborn. I really believed I could find the Port City's Central District and save a few more Islanders.
So why did you just hand this bolt back to me again?
Yes, why? It's only a bolt, after all.
When I first saw this bolt, I wondered why, of all the parts, it was the only relic from the Golden Age. All the other parts of the prosthetic are perfectly ordinary.
When you said your home had been searched by the Inquisition so many times that there were hardly any parts left, I assumed your grandmother had simply made do with what she had.
But for this bolt to have escaped so many searches is unusual in itself, isn't it?
What the Inquisition searches for most strictly is anything made with Islander technology, and anything from the Golden Age.
This bolt happens to be both. And yet it was kept.
"She was clutching that one last bolt, just staring blankly at me"... When you said that, I couldn't help but think of something the Sea Patrol once reported to me.
A technician, already eroded by the Seaborn beyond human shape, was clutching a bottle of plant nutrient solution, just staring blankly at the Sea Patrol commander who was about to kill her.
It was the one thing she still cared about at the very end, after all her consciousness had crumbled—she needed to go feed her most treasured algae one more time.
I think perhaps it was the same for Rufina, and for Aquila.
Rufina hid this bolt from the Inquisition's searches time and time again. Aquila groped across the endless seabed with her bare hands to bring it back.
No matter what was destroyed, no matter how much, this bolt was the last thing they cared about. It was what they felt was most worth keeping—most worth leaving to you.
You said before that what they saw in this bolt was hatred. But I think what they most wanted to leave behind surely wasn't hatred. They'd already poured out far too much hatred as it was.
What they'd held back all these years, wanting to prove but unable to prove no matter how desperately they tried—that is what's worth keeping, and leaving to you.
If all of that is entrusted to one tiny bolt, then this bolt from the Golden Age Port City must have something special about it in itself.
Could you... scan it or something? I don't want to take it apart.
Of course.
Those patterns...
They're Originium circuits for sending and receiving signals.
Even if the Inquisition can't find the Port City's Central District, even if Ægir can't, even if Aulus can't... an old worker who built it with her own hands would still remember where it is.
At this very moment, this bolt is receiving signals from the Port City's Central District, and sending signals to it.
Just as it's been doing for more than seventy years.
Nacho looked at the bolt in his hand, which had been with him for nearly twenty years. It glowed faintly in the dim observation hall.

In that moment, he suddenly realized what that little glimmer of light had been—in the deep of curfew nights, on his cold, hard iron bed, amid the creaking as he tossed and turned, even in his dreams.
Grandma Rufina's love for this land, however little of it remained, had never truly faded.
It was her experience of the Golden Age that made her feel the injustice, and it was that same experience that sustained her defiance.
Seventy years, just like that.
The Port City, it's finished, just like that?
What, you're not happy with it?
No, it's just... can you believe it? We actually built a city this outrageous.
The job's done, so why do you still look like you haven't woken up? Here, take a look at this.
Isn't this one of those bolts we tinkered with together? The King always says in his speeches that the Port City belongs to the Crown—ha! He has no idea what we've driven into it.
This is a secret that only those of us who laid every brick and every tile with our own hands will ever know.
A bolt that glows. Leave it to you to come up with that.
We all came up with it together. If you hadn't told that dumb story about using a light bulb as a float to catch fin, I'd never have thought of such a good idea.
This one in my hand—think of it as a remote switch. I packed a tiny signal receiver inside. Press it once, and every bolt in the Port City will start to glow.
Every bolt in the Port City glowing all at once... what a sight that'd be...
The King can go on about the Port City being his every day if he likes, for all I care. But as long as we press this bolt—
Every person in this city, even every fin in the sea, will see it and know—we came, we were here.
Every brick and every tile of the Port City, every yesterday and every tomorrow it holds—they belong to us.
The young Islander raised the bolt high. She saw her hand pass beyond the sails on the sea, beyond the cranes of the harbor, beyond the flags atop the tall tower.
In the distance, the last bell of dusk had just faded, and the first glow atop the tall tower had just lit up.
The two lights overlapped for a moment, bright as stars.
Bright as stars.
The coordinates of the Port City's Central District!
This bolt really did receive a signal from the Port City's Central District.
If it's still receiving its signal at this very moment... then every bolt in the whole city must already be glowing. Even the Sea Terrors will know—
We came, we were here.
That was the sight Rufina—and so many, many Islanders—wanted everyone to see all their lives. The thing they wanted everyone to know.
They were proud, and they had regrets. They fought hard, and they struggled. They shared beautiful bonds, and they created great things.
Sixty-three years of hostility and slaughter, at the very, very beginning, came from nothing more than the simplest of wishes—
They wanted people to see that they had truly existed, and that their existence had value.
Existed, had value... We did too, right?
That's the one thing I don't need to tell you, Nacho.
The old coordinates named "Rea-Iberia" have been completely erased, and the new coordinates that have just appeared before us don't have a name yet.
Why don't you give them a name?
This bolt was left to you, after all.
The young Islander silently stepped forward.
Almost without thinking, he raised his hand.
In those first few years after I got my prosthetic, when I still couldn't take care of myself, I had a little habit.

I liked looking at things outside the window through its transparent parts. If I just squinted, it was like the fowlbeasts on the branches or the clouds in the distance were right there inside my arm.
Like they belonged to me in that moment. Like I wasn't someone with nothing and nowhere to go.
But I only dared look at insignificant things that way. Fowlbeasts or clouds, or other people's dried fin hung out to dry, or the canvas kites used to collect rain.

If I looked at the people on the street that way, I couldn't help reminding myself that their lives had nothing to do with me in the end. That I was still someone people feared and blamed, someone with nothing and nowhere to go.
There are still lots of people like me.
The people of Iberia—Islanders or anyone else—are all too timid. Even when they fight with everything they have to scrape out a life, they don't dare believe that life belongs to them.
That's why everyone keeps blaming others for taking something from them, and keeps praying for a savior.
But really, no one is anyone's savior, are they? Everything we have is the result of our own struggle.
So, if I'm to give it a name on behalf of everyone...
His hand passed beyond the trenches of the seabed, beyond the turbulent currents of the sea, beyond the towns and villages along the shore...
And covered the brightest point of light. As if the Port City were right there inside his arm.
For a moment, he almost believed—
No. He truly believed.
That point of light—that city, every brick and every tile of it, every yesterday and every tomorrow it held—belonged to him.
It belonged to everyone here, to any one of them here.
The young Islander rose onto his tiptoes, wanting to lift his hand a little higher, to hold that point of light belonging to the Port City more completely within his arm.
Then its name should be—

lines.st: "Our Iberia"

lines.x: Don't hold back, Your Excellency. Feel free to use your handcannon.
Hmph. You're sticking this close to me precisely because you know a handcannon is awkward to use at this range, aren't you?
You caught me. But that's only one of the reasons.
No...
Ngh!
Your close-quarters combat is pretty decent. I'll give you an "excellent" in your file.
Ngh, now the wound's really split wide open. Nando's going to nag me again... Do you know why you lost, Your Excellency?
I was outmatched.
I'd love to say that, but that's not why. You kept shielding that dim lantern of yours, like it was something fragile.
But maybe you didn't notice—while we were trading blows, it got its original light back.
Maybe that won't make you happy, but a High Inquisitor's duty is already carved into your instincts. You value your own survival because you know the duty you carry.
If that's the case, then you should be able to keep going while carrying your mistakes, too. Even if Iberia didn't have a Su Santidad, you could still atone for your own sins.
You really do talk like an instructor.
That's because I am one.
I... made the wrong decision. I'll accept whatever punishment the Inquisition sees fit.
Then why not think first about how to make up for it? Look behind you.
The High Inquisitor turned around. Golden light was bursting forth from the shipyard on the shore.
The golden sea chart hung in the air, and the point of light that had vanished had returned to it once more.
"Our Iberia"... A miracle...
I'd say it's thanks to Supervisor Clementia's efforts. She went to the underwater observation hall alone and came back with good news.
We need to gather enough hands for the salvage. The Inquisition's people alone may not...
When something big comes up, quit thinking the Inquisition's people are the only ones you can use.
Listen. Sounds to me like the shipyard's pretty lively tonight.
Rea-Iberia's coordinates have lit up again, but because the main engine was destroyed, the entire Central District has sunk to the seafloor.
We need to take the boats out to sea right away and tow it back to shore.
But the Port City's Central District is enormous. Without much heavy equipment to help, we need as many hands as possible.
Irene, most of the Inquisition's units are still in the city keeping the people safe. And the number of Seaborn is nothing to scoff at...
Could we conscript the shipyard's craftsmen?
After the Port City's coordinates were erased and the Sea Terrors came ashore, the workers here all evacuated. At this hour, I'm afraid it'll be hard to gather them again...
Which officer said it'd be hard to gather them?
Lost noble and descendant of Iberia's Royal Navy—Estefanía Colón de Toledo, reporting for duty with my naval fleet!
Atonement... atonement... Confess who I really am to my supporters at the shipyard?
No. Sure, I originally claimed to be a noble and recruited a navy just to scrape together enough to live on.
But now that there are people who believe in me and want to hear my stories of the Golden Age, I can't just toss them back into their hard lives.
If someone else ends up like Salvador, ready to throw his life away over a string of beads, they'd be better off running cons with me. At least I can share a meal with them...
What cons?
Salvador? It's dangerous out here. What are you doing outside?
I came to check the sea chart. You said you would light it up. Only once I see the result can I decide whether to believe you.
I broke my word. Not only did I not light up the sea chart, I made the Port City's coordinates disappear. I—
I thought you just hadn't lit it up yet.
Huh?
That's right... It's not that I "didn't" light it up. I just "haven't yet"...
Salvador, do you know where all the shipwrights went to hide?
The shipyard dormitory.
Great. Should I go with you?
You're not going to light up the sea chart?
Forget the sea chart! I'm going to lead you all out to bring back the Port City's Central District ourselves!
All the members of the Royal Navy fleet are here. Officers, we know our way around ships and work at sea. We can help bring the Port City's Central District back.
This... shouldn't be your job.
And you don't even have a lantern between you. Going out to sea in the dead of night is too dangerous. The Inquisition's duty should be to keep you safe first.
But—
If this is your decision, the Inquisition will also protect your freedom to carry it out.
Great!

Don't worry, officers. Every household in Iberia has an oil lamp, and the shipyard keeps plenty in stock too. We can light up the sea and search for traces of the Central District... Huh, where'd my oil lamp go?
Use mine.
Irene?
The Inquisition Messenger withdrew the Arts within her lantern, and the pink flame gradually dimmed.
The lantern in her hand no longer bore any mark of the Inquisition. It was like an oil lamp that could be found in any Iberian's hand.
Meant only to light up the dark.
You can put a match in it, a lump of charcoal, or a dish of fin oil.
It doesn't have the Inquisition's Arts anymore, but it can still light your way.
Thank you, officer!
If we're going to tow the Central District back, besides manpower we'll also need portable anchoring equipment. Do you know how to use it?
More or less. But for salvaging a structure as massive as the Port City's Central District, the equipment's default parameters might not be suitable.
But the only people who know how to adjust the parameters are those Islanders from the Salvage Center...
Anyone can learn to adjust the equipment's parameters, as long as they know the formulas.
We can help adjust them.
Fall in!
Wait.
Everyone, we need to confirm why you're here. We will not treat taking part in the salvage as a bargain at the negotiating table.

We really did hope to use the Port City's Central District to negotiate, to get a chance to be taken seriously in Iberia. And there were times we really did want revenge on the Inquisition and Iberia.

But, at least for now, we want to see what the Port City's Central District that our forebears went on about all their lives actually looks like, and which of the aqueducts they were the ones who built.
After the salvage, we'll decide whether we stay or go.
See, what did I tell you? Islanders and Iberians have always been partners. The Islanders will set sail with the Royal Navy fleet too.
Let's go. To the sea.
The sound of the sea.
Like great waves crashing against reefs, like wooden boats sinking into a fjord. Tefi had been to many places in Iberia, and what she heard today was no different from anything she'd heard before.
So why is my heart leaping like this? she wondered, dazed.
A lamp lit up in the coastal waters. It had no Arts of any kind. It couldn't burn the Sea Terrors, nor could it protect the one who held it. But it shone with a brighter flame.
Held in Tefi's hand, it lit up every salvage boat on the sea, and every person's face.
Before tonight, these supporters of "de Toledo" had undoubtedly seemed foolish and ridiculous to outsiders, and the Islanders accompanying them had seemed dangerous and wicked.
Yet now it was precisely this ragtag "Royal Navy fleet" floating on the perilous sea, and their leader was holding forth just as she always had.
Supporters of House de Toledo, crew of the most exalted fleet, loyal subjects of Iberia!
We are about to raise the old capital of the Golden Age with our own hands. Before we set out, I shall tell you one last story about it—the story of its final curtain.

A descendant of a high-ranking naval officer had the good fortune to escape the terrible Profound Silence. He spent the last of his fortune on a wooden hut in a fin-fishing village, meaning to live out his days in fear.

He kept to the etiquette of a noble, and tending to his uniform became the most important task of his day. He recalled Iberia's past from his journals and refused to admit that the gray sea outside his door had once been the place he longed for.
He walked alone for half a century toward the end of his life, and the last night of his life was a cold, rainy one.

The cold wind crept into the shabby hut he no longer had the strength to repair. With his dim, clouded eyes, he saw a street urchin who'd mistaken his home for an abandoned house and come seeking shelter.
The old officer did not drive her away. Instead, he lit a fire so the two of them could keep warm, and told her the story of his life.

The old officer had never been so happy since the calamity. For the first time, he felt that his memories brought him something other than pain. As for the street urchin, she was utterly enchanted by his stories.
The next day, the old man died, as every man of the Golden Age eventually would. But a new officer who loved telling stories appeared in the village.
This was the final curtain of the Golden Age, and yet also the beginning of another era.
Even if this other era is chaotic, filthy, and dark, it is everything we are living through now. It is every ravaged town. It is tonight.
Can we... really bring back the Port City's Central District... And even if it comes back, will life get any better?
No. Take it from someone who's been through it—nothing gets better right away. It might even stir up more trouble.
That's right. But we're going to pull off something impossible—something worth turning into a story that spreads far and wide.

And then more people will spread these stories, just like that street urchin did, and give a little hope to the struggling Iberians, and a little hope to the Islanders who can't break free of their hatred.
We're good at waiting, good at enduring, because we—or at least some of us—truly believe, deep down, that this place will get better.

Because we're still moved by the stories of the Golden Age and the relics left behind by the Islanders' forebears. Because we never care whether something's true or not. Because a hundred years ago, we already made fantasies come true.
I am Tefi. Even without a family name, I will set sail tonight and raise Rea-Iberia, and make it our dawn, our sun.
All hands! Iberian Civilian Navy Fleet, set sail!
I can't sense the slightest resolve in you, Carmen. Why won't you strike again?!
You can no longer stand steady. If my sword must be used to kill anything, it should be the enemies of Iberia alone, as it has been for the past sixty-three years.
I am your enemy now! One of us is bound to become Iberia's enemy, and the other will become Iberia's Pope.
Listen. Outside.
Shouting, footsteps. Nothing but lost people struggling in vain.
If you truly wish to guide those people, to protect them, you should listen to their voices more closely.
...What they're shouting is... "Salvage the Port City"?
Do you still not understand, Valerio?
Now, no matter which of us walks out of this dungeon, Iberia will not see the birth of a Pope.
No... Draw your sword! It shouldn't end so carelessly like this!
If what you need is to put an end to what happened fifty-three years ago, then I apologize to you, Valerio. Not as a Saint, but as the friend I once was.
I cannot escape the blame for your sacrifice.
You—
But I think that is surely no longer what you need now.
Even now, you still believe that only a common enemy can unite the Iberians, and that only a single Pope can show them the way.
But Iberia no longer needs these things.
Listen. Listen. The Port City has vanished, the Port City has sunk, yet not one person out there is begging for forgiveness or judgment.
They are shouting that they will bring the Port City back with their own hands, even though it is an arduous task that is all but impossible.
Do you think that, at this moment, the Iberians would so much as glance back if one of us walked out of this dungeon covered in blood?
Iberia has already given her answer, in a way far more meaningful than any duel.
Lay down your sword as well, and truly listen to the voice of Iberia.
Just as we used to. It has been many years since I last had a companion at my side, listening with me to this land we love so deeply...
...If it's only for a little while. I can still kill you at any moment.
A little while is enough.
Hey! Do you hear something?
No... Nothing at all...
The people who went out to sea for the salvage haven't come back, and neither have the Inquisition's people...
It's so quiet. Frighteningly quiet. Just like that day sixty-three years ago—
Don't talk nonsense! Even if the Port City's Central District never comes back, we're standing on its Outer District right now. It's all right, we'll be all right...

lines.st: The night shed its unsettling hue, and more and more people stepped out from behind tightly shut doors.
The plaza that had been overrun by Seaborn the night before had regained its calm, and a few Little Helpers were unhurriedly sweeping away the Seaborn remains.
Some were glad they hadn't gotten carried away and joined the salvage crews only to die. Some regretted not saying goodbye to their brave family and friends.
Some lamented that they would never again see Rea-Iberia, more dazzling than the sun. Some simply stood at a loss, fingering the prayer beads in their hands, murmuring a name they did not know.
But the Iberians could not help but walk toward the sea.
As mourners, or as witnesses? No one knew. All they saw was what had once filled them with boundless glory and boundless dread—
The sea.
Before people coveted the riches it held and feared the calamities it carried, their earliest description of it was a breathing, azure land.
And at this moment, it began to breathe more violently than anyone had ever seen. Within the ring of cranes, the surface of the sea swelled high.
Then, in a single instant, the sea's chest burst open.

lines.x: Hundreds of salvage boats drew toward them, hauling salvage cables, like a dense school of fins.
They towed the golden heart of the sea, as if they had hauled up the sun itself.
The people on the shore stood in the cold, "boiling" seawater, bearing witness as Iberia welcomed back its long-lost old capital.
It was unlike any structure in this land today.
Proud spires, banners still white despite having been soaked in seawater for so long, covered bridges leading in every direction, and docks large and small...
Such things had never appeared even in people's dreams, yet now they stood before their very eyes.
They wept. They couldn't put what they felt into words. They were strangely moved by something they had never seen before.
They remembered the song a nameless Iberian had sung in the plaza half a month ago. If they could not speak, then they would sing—
Today a ship sets sail♪
Past the lighthouse, past the church♪
The damp sea mist drifts to the shore♪
"Raise the sails"—the helm's not in the wind's hands♪
Today a ship sets sail♪
A fowlbeast paces on the rail—♪
Let it wait in vain. Sound the horn, haul in the nets♪
We haul up the sun♪
Mentor? You're hurt?
It's a wound I should have received long ago.
And there's no need to call me "Mentor" anymore. For now, I have nothing left to "teach" you.
Uh, Mr. Aulus?
Then, do you need me to find a doctor? Or can your "kin" help you?
There's no need.
It seems the Mutual Aid Society has fallen apart too?
Some went out with the shipyard's shipwrights for the salvage and haven't come back yet.
Some heard the negotiations failed and have already headed north to seek the Iberian Defensa's protection. Some have even decided to join the Church of the Deep.
Some are still undecided, but an Ægir girl came by just now, and she said...
I said that Ægir is willing to offer refuge to any Islanders who don't want to stay in Iberia.
Many years ago, because of the Seaborn's ravages, the first Ægir to leave the home territories had no choice but to come ashore and seek help.
And now, we can take our kin back. We can bring them home.
Thank you, kind young lady. I'll leave these people with me in your care.
If you'd be willing to return to Ægir as well, sir, Milliarium will also provide you with a range of living support and employment guidance.
That won't be necessary for me.
Mr. Aulus? You're abandoning us?
I simply have a road to walk where it wouldn't be convenient to bring you along.
But I won't forget you, nor our "utopia." We'll meet again there.
That day will come.

lines.st: "That storm was truly unforgettable. A whirlpool dozens of times the size of this plaza whipped up waves taller than the cranes behind me."
"Every time that monster-fouled seawater splashed, it stained the sky a little blacker, until at last sky and sea alike were the color of ink—"

lines.x: *Ahem!*
It was in the midst of that very storm that I, Estefanía Colón de Toledo, led the bravest people in this land and found the Port City's Central District.
Whether descendants of the Royal Navy or the children of ordinary fin-fishers, in that moment, all of them were great. Not even our Islander friends were any exception...
Estefanía hasn't changed. If anything, her stories have gotten even more exaggerated.
I think anyone who went through the salvage a few days ago would end up turning what they saw with their own eyes into a story.
Officer Irene, the reason I asked to meet you was to ask about my kin who took part in the attack...
Ms. Tacita is already processing applications from Islanders seeking refuge in Ægir. As long as their crimes aren't serious, they'll be able to return to their homeland soon.
As for the Islanders still hiding in the shadows and harboring resentment toward Iberia, we can't quell their anger. But if they intend to harm Iberia, we certainly won't show them any leniency.
And for the Islanders who tried to take the Port City's Central District hostage but ended up taking part in the salvage, the Inquisition has already handed down its verdict.
Wh-what's going to happen to them...
They will "serve their sentence" in the Port City.
They'll use their own hands to build up this city their forebears built, to make it more like the city the Islanders have always pictured in their hearts—and to make it better.
After all, this place's code name on the sea chart is now "Our Iberia."
Phew... You scared me.
You weren't afraid when a Bishop of the Deep operated on you with a Seaborn, but now you're scared?
You knew?!
Don't worry. Supervisor Clementia has already explained everything to the Inquisition, and now that the Seaborn has been removed from your prosthetic, it won't have any effect on your body.
Yeah. I can finally take a proper look at this city—Rea-Iberia. I can hardly believe it's going to be a real home for me and some of my kin.
Yes. Rea-Iberia is different from every other place in Iberia. It will fully recognize the Islanders as citizens.
And in the rest of Iberia, even if there are obstacles to reshaping how the Islanders are seen, the Inquisition will see it through.
Thank you. And thank the Inquisition for its efforts too.
It's my duty. What do you plan to do next?
I'll keep working here in the Port City. Someday, maybe I'll get to see with my own eyes what the dream Grandma Rufina entrusted to that bolt really looked like.
But before I properly get to work, I need to get my prosthetic repaired first.
Supervisor Clementia recommended a pharmaceutical company to me. I hear they can help me. I think the company is called... Rhodes Island?

...Just when the Penal Battalion and ordinary folk who'd gone to sea in search of the Port City's Central District were about to be swallowed by the storm, a pair of hands and a single lamp showed them the way to safety...
The Iberian people will never abandon their own kin.

lines.st: "The villain never once gave his true heart to his companion. From beginning to end, all he wanted was to extinguish Iberia's light."
"But who can say whether the one who extinguishes the light doesn't mean to kindle another, fiercer fire?"

lines.x: You didn't light a lamp.
Is it that you don't want me to see fire again?
Is this some sort of weak tenderness, or pointless concern? Not seeing fire won't lessen my pain.
After all, the fire in me can never be put out.
So, Carmen, what is it you've come for this time?
I will come often. You needn't search for something to talk about every time.
Will anyone else be coming? Will I become a "teaching aid" for steeling the convictions of new Inquisitors, like that Seaborn before me?
What Iberia needs least now is the conviction to judge others.
For the Port City to become a harbor of Terra once more, much construction work remains to be done, and urgently.
A new fleet will soon be launched. Its sails need no gold or silver embroidery, but they must be strong enough to carry it to far seas that not even the people of the Golden Age ever reached.
After that, Iberia will open its doors to Terra once again.

And how will you deal with that army on the northern border that you have no authority over? For decades, the Iberian Defensa has been convinced that the real threat comes from the foreigners to the north.
They, too, are Iberians. And over these past decades, not a single Iberian has truly been content with the state of this land.
That being so, they too will surely accept change... in one way or another.
You know perfectly well that this "change" of the Iberians' could just as easily end with you hanging from the gallows.
You saw with your own eyes how the people reacted the moment the Port City's Central District rose.
Then you should also know that from now on, they need not live for salvation and judgment. They can simply pursue what is good.
Hanging me from the gallows, I would imagine, is not among those things.
And what of the Inquisition, this organization that bears both glory and sin? How will you explain to the people who revere you that the lights in their hands will gradually fade?
For that matter, I have already found the most suitable person to handle it.
You mean Fidela? Heh, you really have grown merciful. You didn't even dismiss her.
She knows well the anguish of shaken resolve. She will travel across Iberia in my stead, to answer the doubts of soldiers suffering the same anguish, and to show them the way.
I can't even tell whether you truly believe all this, or whether you've merely found an excuse for your final release after such a long ordeal.
You won't live to see any of these futures you dream of with your own eyes, will you?
No matter. This artificial heart of mine will never stop beating.
If Iberia strays from the path, I will correct it.

lines.st: "Just as before, the Iberians once again stood shoulder to shoulder with the visitors from the sea."
"Only this time, they would no longer misunderstand one another. At last, each saw themselves in the other."
"It had always been the same face—a human face."

lines.x: This place really doesn't leak? Or is it that you Ægir don't care if it leaks, since you like soaking in water anyway? Is it true you even built big bathhouses underwater?
Supervisor Clementia's office uses Ægir's latest construction materials and molecular synthesis technology, which can—
All right, all right. Supervisor Clementia, can't you get it to pipe down a little?
Don't you two get along well? I was actually planning to give this Little Helper to you.
...Please don't.
All right, out with it. What did you want me for? You should be up to your neck with the Islander business these days.
I'd like to extend you an offer.
I'm not moving to Ægir, you know. I'm used to living on land. If it's too damp, I'd have to clean my room every week, or else mushrooms start growing.
It's not an offer to relocate. It's a job offer.
I've discussed it with Lord Iberia. We'll be establishing a force based in Rea-Iberia that can legitimately appear anywhere and deal with any problem—the "Land Patrol."
I'd like you to be its captain.
Me?
Yes.
Captain?
That's right.
Sounds like a lot of work.
You're free to decline my offer.
Are you Ægir down in the water really this clueless about how people work? I just need you to give me a way to say yes without losing face.
If it's a way to save face you need... I did bring you something on Lord Iberia's behalf.
Handcannon ammunition engraved with scripture? I thought they only handed these out to Inquisitors who'd earned some merit?
I take it it's not to your liking.
Something this formal and fussy—how about I just toss it for you on my way back?
The Little Helper has a very convenient waste disposal function.
Pfft, I'm joking. Hold on to it. You couldn't become a regular member of the Inquisition before, but at least now Iberia recognizes what you've given. And someday, Ægir will too.
Spoken like someone who's actually been a Consul. You sure know how to talk.
Give me that Little Helper that's been following me around for a week, and I'll say yes.
It seems you've given me a way to save face too.
It's a deal.
I look forward to working with you.
We're connected. Then communications between the defense line and the land should be fully restored.

The Seaborn that cut off communications earlier are fleeing north along the coastline, sweeping up large numbers of other creatures with them. But so far, the Sea Patrol has found no trace of the Bishop of the Deep, Aulus.
...Understood.
You're not going to ask?
Ask about a prisoner whose life isn't even his own to command?
It seems the operation report we received was a polished version. I don't think I need to remind you of the consequences of doing this.
Of course not.

What I can tell you is that when the time is right, the Seaborn-infested coastal waters will be cleared for a while, opening a path to the far side of Terra for Ægir, for Terra, and for Rhodes Island.
At what price?
For Ægir, the right to relocate a volcanic power station that has already been abandoned and no longer functions should hardly count as a price.
You made a deal with Aulus.
I won't hide it from you, Gladiia.
Given his crimes, he has no right to demand anything of Ægir, or of us. But he, too, is searching for a possible path to the future, and this deal also works in our favor in the war.
Are you betting that I won't report you?
Given what we are to each other, I hardly need to put something like this on the table, do I?
...I'll wait until your deal is honored before I make my judgment.
Thank you.
So, is this why you still intend to formally resign as Consul, even after winning your wager with Horatia?
I don't think I need to explain that this in no way means betrayal.
Even if I still have doubts about Ægir's policies, even if my outlook is almost pessimistic, I'd like the Clementia whom Ægir raised to be who she is to respect the rules it has now.
You're different from when you were with Milliarium. Or perhaps you've been different for a long time, and have simply been quietly testing your beliefs for a very, very long time.
Don't worry. My partnership with the Abyssal Hunters still stands, and the Land Patrol will formally establish ties with Ægir later on as well.
Since leaving Ægir, you've hidden your true feelings behind courtesy less often, it seems.
It's nothing.
That's all the information we need to exchange, right?
For now.
Then please allow me to disappear for a while. If you can't reach me for the next forty-eight hours, that's perfectly normal.
You're going to—
Mm.
Phew...
Everything that needed doing should be done, for now...
It's about time I sent my friend at the Academy of Technology some user feedback... The massage strength is still far too weak, no matter what.
And... it worked fine every time before, but this time it feels like something's missing...
After a moment's thought, Clementia gave the Little Helper a command after all.
Little Helper, re-enable the health monitoring module.
—But please don't let it affect the massage function.
Then she peacefully closed her eyes.
Warning: your ECG results show abnormalities. Mild right bundle branch block detected. Recommendation...
Warning: your full-body radiographic imaging shows abnormalities. Coccyx misalignment caused by long-term strain. Recommendation...
Warning: your fin tissue ultrasound shows abnormalities. A nodule of undetermined nature has been found in the head fin. Recommendation...
The Little Helper's warnings went on and on. They were the reality Clementia had deliberately ignored for years.
Iberia, Ægir, the Land Patrol, Rhodes Island, the harbor, uncharted waters... There was still so much for her to deal with. But fortunately, she still had time, and she had people who supported her.
All of it could be left for tomorrow—no, for the day after tomorrow to worry about.
